He took only Peter, and James, and John, with him into that corner of the garden where he suffered his agony. He left the rest at some distance, perhaps at the garden door, with this charge, <hi type="italic">Sit ye here, while I go and pray yonder;</hi> like that of Abraham to his <hi type="italic">young men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.5">Gen. xxii. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">Abide ye here, and I will go yonder and worship.</hi> (1.) Christ went to pray alone, though he had lately prayed with his disciples, <reference osisRef="John.17.1">John xvii. 1</reference>. Note, Our prayers with our families must not excuse us from our secret devotions. (2.) He ordered them to sit here. Note, We must take heed of giving any disturbance or interruption to those who retire for secret communion with God. He took these three with him, because they had been the witnesses of his glory in his transfiguration (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.1-Matt.17.2">ch. xvii. 1, 2</reference>), and that would prepare them to be the witnesses of his agony. Note, Those are best prepared to suffer with Christ, that have by faith beheld his glory, and have conversed with the glorified saints upon the holy mount. <hi type="italic">If we suffer with Christ, we shall reign with him;</hi> and if we hope to reign with him, why should we not expect to suffer with him? <div eID="gen23909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23910" type="x-p"/> III. The agony itself that he was in; <hi type="italic">He began to be sorrowful, and very heavy.</hi> It is called an agony (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.44">Luke xxii. 44</reference>), a conflict. It was not any bodily pain or torment that he was in, nothing occurred to hurt him; but, whatever it was, it was from within; he troubled himself, <reference osisRef="John.11.33">John xi. 33</reference>. The words here used are very emphatical; he began <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">lupeisthai kai ademunein</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">to be sorrowful, and in a consternation.</hi> The latter word signifies such a sorrow as makes a man neither fit for company nor desirous of it. He had like a weight of lead upon his spirits. Physicians use a word near akin to it, to signify the disorder a man is in in a fit of an ague, or beginning of a fever. Now was fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.14">Ps. xxii. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">I am poured out like water, my heart is like wax, it is melted;</hi> and all those passages in the Psalms where David complains of the sorrows of his soul, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.4-Ps.18.5 Ps.42.7 Ps.55.4-Ps.55.5 Ps.69.1-Ps.69.3">Ps. xviii. 4, 5; xlii. 7; lv. 4, 5; lxix. 1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.3">lxxxviii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.3">cxvi. 3</reference>, and Jonah's complaint, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.4-Jonah.2.5">ch. ii. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen23910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23911" type="x-p"/> But what was the cause of all this? What was it that put him into his agony? <hi type="italic">Why art thou cast down,</hi> blessed Jesus, and <hi type="italic">why disquieted?</hi> Certainly, it was nothing of despair or distrust of his Father, much less any conflict or struggle with him. As the Father loved him because he laid down his life for the sheep, so he was entirely subject to his Father's will in it. But, <div eID="gen23911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23912" type="x-p"/> 1. He engaged in an encounter with the powers of darkness; so he intimates (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.53">Luke xxii. 53</reference>); <hi type="italic">This is your hour, and the power of darkness:</hi> and he spoke of it just before (<reference osisRef="John.14.30-John.14.31">John xiv. 30, 31</reference>); "<hi type="italic">The prince of this world cometh.</hi> I see him rallying his forces, and preparing for a general assault; but <hi type="italic">he has nothing in me,</hi> no garrisons in his interest, none that secretly hold correspondence with him; and therefore his attempts, though fierce, will be fruitless: but <hi type="italic">as the Father gave me commandment, so I do;</hi> however it be, I must have a struggle with him, the field must be fairly fought; and therefore <hi type="italic">arise, let us go hence,</hi> let us hasten to the field of battle, and meet the enemy." Now is the close engagement in single combat between Michael and the dragon, hand to hand; <hi type="italic">now is the judgment of this world;</hi> the great cause is now to be determined, and the decisive battle fought, in which the <hi type="italic">prince of this world,</hi> will certainly be beaten and <hi type="italic">cast out,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.31">John xii. 31</reference>. Christ, when he works salvation, is described like a champion taking the field, <reference osisRef="Isa.59.16-Isa.59.18">Isa. lix. 16-18</reference>. Now the serpent makes his fiercest onset on the seed of the woman, and directs his sting, the sting of death, to his very heart; <hi type="italic">animamque in vulnere ponit—and the wound is mortal.</hi> <div eID="gen23912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23913" type="x-p"/> 2. He was now <hi type="italic">bearing the iniquities</hi> which the Father laid upon him, and, by his sorrow and amazement, he accommodated himself to his undertaking. The sufferings he was entering upon were for our sins; they were all made to meet upon him, and he knew it. As we are obliged to be sorry for our particular sins, so was he grieved for the sins of us all. So Bishop Pearson, p. 191. Now, <hi type="italic">in the valley of Jehoshaphat,</hi> where Christ now was, God <hi type="italic">gathered all nations,</hi> and <hi type="italic">pleaded with them in his</hi> Son, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.2">Joel iii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.12">12</reference>. He knew the malignity of the sins that were laid upon him, how provoking to God, how ruining to man; and these being all set in order before him, and charged upon him, he was <hi type="italic">sorrowful and very heavy.</hi> Now it was that <hi type="italic">iniquities took hold on him;</hi> so that he was <hi type="italic">not able to look up,</hi> as was foretold concerning him, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Ps. xl. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.12">12</reference>. <div eID="gen23913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23914" type="x-p"/> 3. He had a full and clear prospect of all the sufferings that were before him. He foresaw the treachery of Judas, the unkindness of Peter, the malice of the Jews, and their base ingratitude. He knew that he should now in a few hours be scourged, spit upon, crowned with thorns, nailed to the cross; death in its most dreadful appearances, death in pomp, attended with all its terrors, looked him in the face; and this made him sorrowful, especially because it was the wages of our sin, which he had undertaken to satisfy for. It is true, the martyrs that have suffered for Christ, have entertained the greatest torments, and the most terrible deaths, without any such sorrow and consternation; have called their prisons their delectable orchards, and a bed of flames a bed of roses: but then, (1.) Christ was now denied the supports and comforts which they had; that is, he denied them to himself, and <hi type="italic">his soul refused to be comforted,</hi> not in passion, but in justice to his undertaking. Their cheerfulness under the cross was owing to the divine favour, which, for the present, was suspended from the Lord Jesus. (2.) His sufferings were of another nature from theirs. St. Paul, when he is to be offered upon the sacrifice and service of the saints' faith, can <hi type="italic">joy and rejoice with them all;</hi> but to be offered a sacrifice, to make atonement for sin, is quite a different case. On the saints' cross there is a blessing pronounced, which enables them to rejoice under it (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.10">ch. v. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.12">12</reference>); but to Christ's cross there was a curse annexed, which made him sorrowful and very heavy under it. And his sorrow under the cross was the foundation of their joy under it. <div eID="gen23914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23915" type="x-p"/> IV. His complaint of this agony. Finding himself under the arrest of his passion, he goes to his disciples (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.38">v. 38</reference>), and, <div eID="gen23915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23916" type="x-p"/> 1. He acquaints them with his condition; <hi type="italic">My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death.</hi> It gives some little ease to a troubled spirit, to have a friend ready to unbosom itself to, and give vent to its sorrows. Christ here tells them, (1.) What was the seat of his sorrow; it was his soul that was now in an agony. This proves that Christ had a true human soul; for he suffered, not only in his body, but in his soul. We had sinned both against our own bodies, and against our souls; both had been used in sin, and both had been wronged by it; and therefore Christ suffered in soul as well as in body. (2.) What was the degree of his sorrow. He was <hi type="italic">exceedingly sorrowful,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">perilypos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">compassed about with sorrow on all hands.</hi> It was sorrow in the highest degree, even unto death; it was a killing sorrow, such sorrow as no mortal man could bear and live. He was ready to die for grief; they were sorrows of death. (3.) The duration of it; it will continue even unto death. "My soul will be sorrowful as long as it is in this body; I see no outlet but death." He now <hi type="italic">began</hi> to be sorrowful, and never ceased to be so till he said, <hi type="italic">It is finished;</hi> that grief is now finished, which began in the garden. It was prophesied of Christ, that he should be <hi type="italic">a Man of sorrows</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.3">Isa. liii. 3</reference>); he was so all along, we never read that he laughed; but all his sorrows hitherto were nothing to this. <div eID="gen23916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23917" type="x-p"/> 2. He bespeaks their company and attendance; <hi type="italic">Tarry ye here, and watch with me.</hi> Surely he was destitute indeed of help, when he entreated theirs, who, he knew, would be but miserable comforters; but he would hereby teach us the benefit of the communion of saints. It is good to have, and therefore good to seek, the assistance of our brethren, when at any time we are in an agony; <hi type="italic">for two are better than one.</hi> What he said to them, he saith to all, <hi type="italic">Watch,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.13.37">Mark xiii. 37</reference>. Not only watch for him, in expectation of his future coming, but watch with him, in application to our present work. <div eID="gen23917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23918" type="x-p"/> V. What passed between him and his Father when he was in this agony; <hi type="italic">Being in an agony, he prayed.</hi> Prayer is never out of season, but it is especially seasonable in an agony. <div eID="gen23918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23919" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. The place where he prayed; <hi type="italic">He went a little further,</hi> withdrew from them, that the scripture might be fulfilled, <hi type="italic">I have trod the wine-press alone;</hi> he retired for prayer; a troubled soul finds most ease when it is alone with God, who understands the broken language of sighs and groans. Calvin's devout remark upon this is worth transcribing, <hi type="italic">Utile est seorsim orare, tunc enim magis familiariter sese denudat fidelis animus, et simplicius sua vota, gemitus, curas, pavores, spes, et gaudia in Dei sinum exonerat—It is useful to pray apart; for then the faithful soul develops itself more familiarly, and with greater simplicity pours forth its petitions, groans, cares, fears, hopes and joys, into the bosom of God.</hi> Christ has hereby taught us that secret prayer must be made secretly. Yet some think that even the disciples whom he left at the garden door, overheard him; for it is said (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>), they were <hi type="italic">strong cries.</hi> <div eID="gen23919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23920" type="x-p"/> 2. His posture in prayer; <hi type="italic">He fell on his face;</hi> his lying prostrate denotes, (1.) The agony he was in, and the extremity of his sorrow. Job, in great grief, <hi type="italic">fell on the ground;</hi> and great anguish is expressed by <hi type="italic">rolling in the dust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.1.10">Mic. i. 10</reference>. (2.) His humility in prayer. This posture was an expression of his, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eulabeia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">his reverential fear</hi> (spoken of <reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>), with which he offered up these prayers: and it was <hi type="italic">in the days of his flesh,</hi> in his estate of humiliation, to which hereby he accommodated himself. <div eID="gen23920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23921" type="x-p"/> 3. The prayer itself; wherein we may observe three things. <div eID="gen23921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23922" type="x-p"/> (1.) The title he gives to God; <hi type="italic">O my Father.</hi> Thick as the cloud was, he could see God as a Father through it. Note, In all our addresses to God we should eye him as a Father, as our Father; and it is in a special manner comfortable to do so, when we are in an agony. It is a pleasing string to harp upon at such a time, <hi type="italic">My Father;</hi> whither should the child go, when any thing grieves him, but to his father? <div eID="gen23922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23923" type="x-p"/> (2.) The favour he begs; <hi type="italic">If it be possible, let this cup pass from me.</hi> He calls his sufferings a <hi type="italic">cup;</hi> not a river, not a sea, but a cup, which we shall soon see the bottom of. When we are under troubles, we should make the best, the least, of them, and not aggravate them. His sufferings might be called a <hi type="italic">cup,</hi> because allotted him, as at feasts a cup was set to every mess. He begs that this cup might <hi type="italic">pass from him,</hi> that is, that he might avoid the sufferings now at hand; or, at least, that they might be shortened. This intimates no more than that he was really and truly Man, and as a Man he could not but be averse to pain and suffering. This is the first and simple act of man's will—to start back from that which is sensibly grievous to us, and to desire the prevention and removal of it. The law of self-preservation is impressed upon the innocent nature of man, and rules there till overruled by some other law; therefore Christ admitted and expressed a reluctance to suffer, to show that he was <hi type="italic">taken from among men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.1">Heb. v. 1</reference>), was touched with <hi type="italic">the feeling of our infirmities</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.15">Heb. iv. 15</reference>), and <hi type="italic">tempted as we are; yet without sin.</hi> Note, A prayer of faith against an affliction, may very well consist with the patience of hope under affliction. When David had said, <hi type="italic">I was dumb, I opened not my mouth, because thou didst it;</hi> his very next words were, <hi type="italic">Remove thy stroke away from me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.39.9-Ps.39.10">Ps. xxxix. 9, 10</reference>. But observe the proviso; <hi type="italic">If it be possible.</hi> If God may be glorified, man saved, and the ends of his undertaking answered, without his drinking of this bitter cup, he desires to be excused; otherwise not. What we cannot do with the securing of our great end, we must reckon to be in effect impossible; Christ did so. <hi type="italic">Id possumus quod jure possumus—We can do that which we can do lawfully.</hi> We <hi type="italic">can</hi> do nothing, not only we <hi type="italic">may</hi> do nothing, against the truth. <div eID="gen23923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23924" type="x-p"/> (3.) His entire submission to, and acquiescence in, the will of God; <hi type="italic">Nevertheless, not as I will, but as thou wilt.</hi> Not that the human will of Christ was adverse or averse to the divine will; it was only, in its first act, diverse from it; to which, in the second act of the will, which compares and chooses, he freely submits himself. Note, [1.] Our Lord Jesus, though he had a quick sense of the extreme bitterness of the sufferings he was to undergo, yet was freely willing to submit to them for our redemption and salvation, and <hi type="italic">offered himself, and gave himself, for us.</hi> [2.] The reason of Christ's submission to his sufferings, was, his Father's will; <hi type="italic">as thou wilt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.26.39">v. 39</reference>. He grounds his own willingness upon the Father's will, and resolves the matter wholly into that; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he did what he did, and did it with delight, because it was the will of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.8">Ps. xl. 8</reference>. This he had often referred to, as that which put him upon, and carried him through, his whole undertaking; <hi type="italic">This is the Father's will,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.39-John.6.40">John vi. 39, 40</reference>. This he sought (<reference osisRef="John.5.30">John v. 30</reference>); it was his <hi type="italic">meat and drink</hi> to do it, <reference osisRef="John.4.34">John iv. 34</reference>. [3.] In conformity to this example of Christ, we must drink of the bitter cup which God puts into our hands, be it ever so bitter; though nature struggle, grace must submit. We then are disposed as Christ was, when our wills are in every thing melted into the will of God, though ever so displeasing to flesh and blood; <hi type="italic">The will of the Lord be done,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.21.14">Acts xxi. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen23924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23925" type="x-p"/> 4. The repetition of the prayer; <hi type="italic">He went away again the second time, and prayed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.42">v. 42</reference>), and again the third time (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.44">v. 44</reference>), and all to the same purport; only, as it is related here, he did not, in the second and third prayer, expressly ask that the cup might pass from him, as he had done in the first. Note, Though we may pray to God to prevent and remove an affliction, yet our chief errand, and that which we should most insist upon, must be, that he will give us grace to bear it well. It should be more our care to get our troubles sanctified, and our hearts satisfied under them, than to get them taken away. <hi type="italic">He prayed, saying, Thy will be done.</hi> Note, Prayer is the offering up, not only of our desires, but of our resignations, to God. It amounts to an acceptable prayer, when at any time we are in distress, to refer ourselves to God, and to commit our way and work to him; <hi type="italic">Thy will be done.</hi> The third time he <hi type="italic">said the same words,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ton auton logon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the same word,</hi> that is the same matter or argument; he spoke to the same purport. We have reason to think that this was not all he said, for it should seem by <reference osisRef="Matt.26.40">v. 40</reference> that he continued <hi type="italic">an hour</hi> in his agony and prayer; but, whatever more he said, it was to this effect, deprecating his approaching sufferings, and yet resigning himself to God's will in them, in the expressions of which we may be sure he was not straitened. <div eID="gen23925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23926" type="x-p"/> But what answer had he to this prayer? Certainly it was not made in vain; he that heard him <hi type="italic">always,</hi> did not deny him <hi type="italic">now.</hi> It is true, the cup did not pass from him, for he withdrew that petition, and did not insist upon it (if he had, for aught I know, the cup had passed away); but he had an answer to his prayer; for, (1.) <hi type="italic">He was strengthened with strength in his soul,</hi> in the day when he cried (<reference osisRef="Ps.138.3">Ps. cxxxviii. 3</reference>); and that was a real answer, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.43">Luke xxii. 43</reference>. (2.) He was delivered from that which he feared, which was, lest by impatience and distrust he should offend his Father, and so disable himself to go on with his undertaking, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>. In answer to his prayer, God provided that he should not fail or be discouraged. <div eID="gen23926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23927" type="x-p"/> VI. What passed between him and his three disciples at this time; and here we may observe, <div eID="gen23927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23928" type="x-p"/> 1. The fault they were guilty of; that when he was in his agony, sorrowful and heavy, sweating and wrestling and praying, they were so little concerned, that they could not keep awake; he comes, and <hi type="italic">finds them asleep,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.26.40">v. 40</reference>. The strangeness of the thing should have roused their spirits to <hi type="italic">turn aside now, and see this great sight—the bush burning, and yet not consumed;</hi> much more should their love to their Master, and their care concerning him, have obliged them to a more close and vigilant attendance on him; yet they were so dull, that they could not keep their eyes open. What had become of us, if Christ had been now as sleepy as his disciples were? It is well for us that our salvation is in the hand of one who <hi type="italic">neither slumbers nor sleeps.</hi> Christ engaged them to watch with him, as if he expected some succour from them, and yet they slept; surely it was the unkindest thing that could be. When David wept at this mount of Olives, all his followers wept with him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2 Sam. xv. 30</reference>); but when the Son of David was here in tears, his followers were asleep. His enemies, who watched for him, were wakeful enough (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.43">Mark xiv. 43</reference>); but his disciples, who should have watched with him, were asleep. Lord, what is man! What are the best of men, when God leaves them to themselves! Note, Carelessness and carnal security, especially when Christ is in his agony, are great faults in any, but especially in those who profess to be nearest in relation to him. The church of Christ, which is his body, is often in an agony, fightings without and fears within; and shall we be asleep then, like Gallio, that <hi type="italic">cared for none of these things;</hi> or those (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.6">Amos vi. 6</reference>) that <hi type="italic">lay at ease, and were not grieved for the affliction of Joseph?</hi> <div eID="gen23928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23929" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ's favour to them, notwithstanding. Persons in sorrow are too apt to be cross and peevish with those about them, and to lay it grievously to heart, if they but seem to neglect them; but Christ in his agony is as meek as ever, and carries it as patiently toward his followers as toward his Father, and is not apt to take things ill. <div eID="gen23929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23930" type="x-p"/> When Christ's disciples put this slight upon him, <div eID="gen23930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23931" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">He came to them,</hi> as if he expected to receive some comfort from them; and if they had put him in mind of what they had heard from him concerning his resurrection and glory perhaps it might have been some help to him; but, instead of that, they added grief to his sorrow; and yet he came to them, more careful for them than they were for themselves; when he was most engaged, yet he came to look after them; for those that were given him, were upon his heart, living and dying. <div eID="gen23931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23932" type="x-p"/> (2.) He gave them a gentle reproof, for as many as he loves he rebukes; he directed it to Peter, who used to <hi type="italic">speak</hi> for them; let him now <hi type="italic">hear</hi> for them. The reproof was very melting; <hi type="italic">What! could ye not watch with me one hour?</hi> He speaks as one amazed to see them so stupid; every word, when closely considered, shows the aggravated nature of the case. Consider, [1.] Who <hi type="italic">they</hi> were; "Could not <hi type="italic">ye</hi> watch—ye, my disciples and followers? No wonder if others neglect me, if <hi type="italic">the earth sit still, and be at rest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.11">Zech. i. 11</reference>); but from you I expected better things." [2.] Who <hi type="italic">he</hi> was; "Watch with <hi type="italic">me.</hi> If one of yourselves were ill and in an agony, it would be very unkind not to watch with him; but it is undutiful not to watch with your Master, who has long watched over you for good, has led you, and fed you, and taught you, borne you, and borne with you; do ye thus requite him?" He awoke out of his sleep, to help them when they were in distress (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.26">ch. viii. 26</reference>); and could not they keep awake, at least to show their good-will to him, especially considering that he was now suffering <hi type="italic">for them,</hi> in an agony <hi type="italic">for them? Jam tua res agiture—I am suffering in your cause.</hi> [3.] How small a thing it was that he expected from them—only to <hi type="italic">watch with him.</hi> If he had bid them do some great thing, had bid them be in an agony with him, or die with him, they thought they could have done it; and yet they could not do it, when he only desired them to <hi type="italic">watch with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.13">2 Kings v. 13</reference>. [4.] How short a time it was that he expected it—but <hi type="italic">one hour;</hi> they were not set upon the guard whole nights, as the prophet was (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.8">Isa. xxi. 8</reference>), only <hi type="italic">one hour.</hi> Sometimes he <hi type="italic">continued all night in prayer to God,</hi> but did not then expect that his disciples should watch with him; only now, when he had but one hour to spend in prayer. <div eID="gen23932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23933" type="x-p"/> (3.) He gave them good counsel; <hi type="italic">Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.26.41">v. 41</reference>. [1.] There was an hour of temptation drawing on, and very near; the troubles of Christ were temptations to his followers to disbelieve and distrust him, to deny and desert him, and renounce all relation to him. [2.] There was danger of their entering into the temptation, as into a snare or trap; of their entering into a parley with it, or a good opinion of it, of their being influenced by it, and inclining to comply with it; which is the first step toward being overcome by it. [3.] He therefore exhorts them to watch and pray; <hi type="italic">Watch with me, and pray with me.</hi> While they were sleeping, they lost the benefit of joining in Christ's prayer. "Watch <hi type="italic">yourselves,</hi> and pray <hi type="italic">yourselves.</hi> Watch and pray against this present temptation to drowsiness and security; <hi type="italic">pray</hi> that you may <hi type="italic">watch;</hi> beg of God by his grace to keep you awake, now that there is occasion." When we are drowsy in the worship of God, we should pray, as a good Christian once did, "The Lord deliver me from this sleepy devil!" <hi type="italic">Lord, quicken thou me in thy way,</hi> Or, "Watch and pray against the further temptation you may be assaulted with; <hi type="italic">watch and pray</hi> lest this sin prove the inlet of many more." Note, When we find ourselves entering into temptation, we have need to watch and pray. <div eID="gen23933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23934" type="x-p"/> (4.) He kindly excused for them; <hi type="italic">The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.</hi> We do not read of one word they had to say for themselves (the sense of their own weakness stopped their mouth); but then he had a tender word to say on their behalf, for it is his office to be an Advocate; in this he sets us an example of the love <hi type="italic">which covers a multitude of sins.</hi> He considered their frame, and did not chide them, for he remembered that they were but flesh; <hi type="italic">and the flesh is weak, though the spirit be willing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.38-Ps.78.39">Ps. lxxviii. 38, 39</reference>. Note, [1.] Christ's disciples, as long as they are here in this world, have bodies as well as souls, and a principle of remaining corruption as well as of reigning grace, like Jacob and Esau in the same womb, <hi type="italic">Canaanites</hi> and <hi type="italic">Israelites</hi> in the same land, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.17">Gal. v. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.24">24</reference>. [2.] It is the unhappiness and burthen of Christ's disciples, that their bodies cannot keep pace with their souls in works of piety and devotion, but are many a time a cloud and clog to them; that, when the spirit is free and disposed to that which is good, the flesh is averse and indisposed. This St. Paul laments (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.25">Rom. vii. 25</reference>); <hi type="italic">With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin.</hi> Our impotency in the service of God is the great iniquity and infidelity of our nature, and it arises from these sad remainders of corruption, which are the constant grief and burthen of God's people. [3.] Yet it is our comfort, that our Master graciously considers this, and accepts the willingness of the spirit, and pities and pardons the weakness and infirmity of the flesh; for <hi type="italic">we are under grace, and not under the law.</hi> <div eID="gen23934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23935" type="x-p"/> (5.) Though they continued dull and sleepy, he did not any further rebuke them for it; for, though we daily offend, yet he will not always chide. [1.] When he came to them the second time, we do not find that he said any thing to them (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.43">v. 43</reference>); <hi type="italic">he findeth them asleep again.</hi> One would have thought that he had said enough to them to keep them awake; but it is hard to recover from a spirit of slumber. Carnal security, when once it prevails, is not easily shaken off. <hi type="italic">Their eyes were heavy,</hi> which intimates that they strove against it as much as they could, but were overcome by it, like the spouse; <hi type="italic">I sleep, but my heart waketh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.5.2">Cant. v. 2</reference>); and therefore their Master looked upon them with compassion. [2.] When he came the third time, he left them to be alarmed with the approaching danger (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.45-Matt.26.46">v. 45, 46</reference>); <hi type="italic">Sleep on now, and take your rest.</hi> This is spoken ironically; "Now sleep if you can, sleep if you dare; I would not disturb you if Judas and his band of men would not." See here how Christ deals with those that suffer themselves to be overcome by security, and will not be awakened out of it. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Sometimes he gives them up to the power of it; <hi type="italic">Sleep on now.</hi> He that will sleep, let him sleep still. The curse of spiritual slumber is the just punishment of the sin of it, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.8">Rom. xi. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.17">Hos. iv. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Many times he sends some startling judgment, to awaken those that would not be wrought upon by the word; and those who will not be alarmed by reasons and arguments, had better be alarmed by swords and spears than left to perish in their security. Let those that would not believe, be made to feel. <div eID="gen23935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23936" type="x-p"/> As to the disciples here, 1. Their Master gave them notice of the near approach of his enemies, who, it is likely, were now within sight or hearing, for they came with candles and torches, and, it is likely, made a great noise; <hi type="italic">The Son of man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.</hi> And again, <hi type="italic">He is at hand that doth betray me.</hi> Note, Christ's sufferings were no surprise to him; he knew what, and when, he was to suffer. By this time the extremity of his agony was pretty well over, or, at least, diverted; while with an undaunted courage he addresses himself to the next encounter, as a champion to the combat. 2. He called them to rise, and be going: not, "Rise, and let us flee from the danger;" but, "Rise, and let us go meet it;" before he had prayed, he feared his sufferings, but now he had got over his fears. But, 3. He intimates to them their folly, in sleeping away the time which they should have spent in preparation; now the event found them unready, and was a terror to them.
entries.74ac0f7265111217dccd824eff27d0ba903f0c6c: <div eID="gen23936" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Betrayed by Judas; The Priest's Servant Smitten by Peter; Christ Deserted by His Disciples.</title> <div sID="gen23937" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">47</hi> And while he yet spake, lo, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great multitude with swords and staves, from the chief priests and elders of the people. <hi type="super">48</hi> Now he that betrayed him gave them a sign, saying, Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he: hold him fast. <hi type="super">49</hi> And forthwith he came to Jesus, and said, Hail, master; and kissed him. <hi type="super">50</hi> And Jesus said unto him, Friend, wherefore art thou come? Then came they, and laid hands on Jesus, and took him. <hi type="super">51</hi> And, behold, one of them which were with Jesus stretched out <hi type="italic">his</hi> hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest's, and smote off his ear. <hi type="super">52</hi> Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword. <hi type="super">53</hi> Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels? <hi type="super">54</hi> But how then shall the scriptures be fulfilled, that thus it must be? <hi type="super">55</hi> In that same hour said Jesus to the multitudes, Are ye come out as against a thief with swords and staves for to take me? I sat daily with you teaching in the temple, and ye laid no hold on me. <hi type="super">56</hi> But all this was done, that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Then all the disciples forsook him, and fled. <div eID="gen23937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23938" type="x-p"/> We are here told how the blessed Jesus was seized, and taken into custody; this followed immediately upon his agony, <hi type="italic">while he yet spake;</hi> for from the beginning to the close of his passion he had not the least intermission or breathing-time, but <hi type="italic">deep called unto deep.</hi> His trouble hitherto was raised within himself; but now the scene is changed, now the Philistines are upon thee, thou blessed Samson; <hi type="italic">the Breath of our nostrils, the Anointed of the Lord is taken in their pits,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.4.20">Lam. iv. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen23938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23939" type="x-p"/> Now concerning the apprehension of the Lord Jesus, observe, <div eID="gen23939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23940" type="x-p"/> I. Who the persons were, that were employed in it. 1. Here was <hi type="italic">Judas, one of the twelve,</hi> at the head of this infamous guard: <hi type="italic">he was guide to them that took Jesus</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.16">Acts i. 16</reference>); without his help they could not have found him in this retirement. Behold, and wonder; the first that appears with his enemies, is one of his own disciples, who an hour or two ago was eating bread with him! 2. Here was <hi type="italic">with him a great multitude;</hi> that the scripture might be fulfilled, <hi type="italic">Lord, how are they increased that trouble me!</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.3.1">Ps. iii. 1</reference>. This multitude was made up partly of a detachment out of the guards, that were posted in the tower of Antonia by the Roman governor; these were Gentiles, <hi type="italic">sinners,</hi> as Christ calls them, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.45">v. 45</reference>. The rest were the servants and officers of the High Priest, and they were Jews; they that were at variance with each other, agreed against Christ. <div eID="gen23940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23941" type="x-p"/> II. How they were armed for this enterprise. <div eID="gen23941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23942" type="x-p"/> 1. What weapons they were armed with; They came <hi type="italic">with swords and staves.</hi> The Roman soldiers, no doubt, had swords; the servants of the priests, those of them that had not swords, brought staves or clubs. <hi type="italic">Furor arma ministrat—Their rage supplied their arms.</hi> They were not regular troops, but a tumultuous rabble. But wherefore is this ado? If they had been ten times as many, they could not have taken him had he not yielded; and, his hour being come for him to give up himself, all this force was needless. When a butcher goes into the field to take out a lamb for the slaughter, does he raise the militia, and come armed? No, he needs not; yet is there all this force used to seize the Lamb of God. <div eID="gen23942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23943" type="x-p"/> 2. What warrant they were armed with; <hi type="italic">They came from the chief priests, and elders of the people;</hi> this armed multitude was sent by them upon this errand. He was taken up by a warrant from the great sanhedrim, as a person obnoxious to them. Pilate, the Roman governor, gave them no warrant to search for him, he had no jealousy of him; but they were men who pretended to religion, and presided in the affairs of the church, that were active in this prosecution, and were the most spiteful enemies Christ had. It was a sign that he was supported by a divine power, for by all earthly powers he was not only deserted, but opposed; Pilate upbraided him with it; <hi type="italic">Thine own nation and the chief priests delivered thee to me,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.18.35">John xviii. 35</reference>. <div eID="gen23943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23944" type="x-p"/> III. The manner how it was done, and what passed at that time. <div eID="gen23944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23945" type="x-p"/> 1. How Judas betrayed him; he did his business effectually, and his resolution in this wickedness may shame us who fail in that which is good. Observe, <div eID="gen23945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23946" type="x-p"/> (1.) The instructions he gave to the soldiers (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.48">v. 48</reference>); <hi type="italic">He gave them a sign;</hi> as commander of the party in this action, he gives the word or signal. He <hi type="italic">gave them a sign,</hi> lest by mistake they should seize one of the disciples instead of him, the disciples having so lately said, in Judas's hearing, that they would be willing to die for him. What abundance of caution was here, not to miss him—<hi type="italic">That same is he;</hi> and when they had him in their hands, not to lose him—<hi type="italic">Hold him fast;</hi> for he had sometimes escaped from those who thought to secure him; as <reference osisRef="Luke.6.30">Luke vi. 30</reference>. Though the Jews, who frequented the temple, could not but know him, yet the Roman soldiers perhaps had never seen him, and the sign was to direct them; and Judas by his kiss intended not only to distinguish him, but to detain him, while they came behind him, and laid hands on him. <div eID="gen23946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23947" type="x-p"/> (2.) The dissembling compliment he gave his Master. He came close up to Jesus; surely now, if ever, his wicked heart will relent; surely when he comes to look him in the face, he will either be awed by its majesty, or charmed by its beauty. Dares he to come into his very sight and presence, to betray him? Peter denied Christ, but when <hi type="italic">the Lord turned and looked</hi> upon him, he relented presently; but Judas comes up to his Master's face, and betrays him. <hi type="italic">Me mihi (perfide) prodis? me mihi prodis?—Perfidious man, betrayest thou me to thyself?</hi> He said, <hi type="italic">Hail, Master; and kissed him.</hi> It should seem, our Lord Jesus had been wont to admit his disciples to such a degree of familiarity with him, as to give them his cheek to kiss after they had been any while absent, which Judas villainously used to facilitate this treason. A kiss is a token of allegiance and friendship, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">Ps. ii. 12</reference>. But Judas, when he broke all the laws of love and duty, profaned this sacred sign to serve his purpose. Note, There are many that betray Christ with <hi type="italic">a kiss,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Hail, Master;</hi> who, under pretence of doing him honour, betray and undermine the interests of his kingdom. <hi type="italic">Mel in ore, fel in corde—Honey in the mouth, gall in the heart.</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Kataphilein ouk esti philein.</hi></hi> <hi type="italic">To embrace is one thing, to love is another. Philo Judæus.</hi> Joab's kiss and Judas's were much alike. <div eID="gen23947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23948" type="x-p"/> (3.) The entertainment his Master gave him, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.50">v. 50</reference>. <div eID="gen23948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23949" type="x-p"/> [1.] He calls him <hi type="italic">friend.</hi> If he had called him <hi type="italic">villain,</hi> and <hi type="italic">traitor, raca, thou fool,</hi> and <hi type="italic">child of the devil,</hi> he had not <hi type="italic">mis—</hi>called him; but he would teach us under the greatest provocation to forbear bitterness and evil-speaking, and to show all meekness. <hi type="italic">Friend,</hi> for a friend he had been, and should have been, and seemed to be. Thus he upbraids him, as Abraham, when he called the rich man in hell, <hi type="italic">son.</hi> He calls him <hi type="italic">friend,</hi> because he furthered his sufferings, and so <hi type="italic">befriended</hi> him; whereas, he called Peter <hi type="italic">Satan</hi> for attempting to hinder them. <div eID="gen23949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23950" type="x-p"/> [2.] He asks him, "<hi type="italic">Wherefore art thou come?</hi> Is it peace, Judas? Explain thyself; if thou come as an enemy, what means this kiss? If as a friend, what mean these swords and staves? <hi type="italic">Wherefore art thou come?</hi> What harm have I done thee? Wherein have I wearied thee? <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eph ho parei</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Wherefore art thou present?</hi> Why hadst thou not so much shame left thee, as to keep out of sight, which thou mightest have done, and yet have given the officer notice where I was?" This was an instance of great impudence, for him to be so forward and barefaced in this wicked transaction. But it is usual for apostates from religion to be the most bitter enemies to it; witness Julian. Thus Judas did his part. <div eID="gen23950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23951" type="x-p"/> 2. How the officers and soldiers secured him; <hi type="italic">Then came they, and laid hands on Jesus, and took him;</hi> they made him their prisoner. <hi type="italic">How were they not afraid to stretch forth their hands against the Lord's Anointed?</hi> We may well imagine what rude and cruel hands they were, which this barbarous multitude laid on Christ; and how, it is probable, they handled him the more roughly for their being so often disappointed when they sought to lay hands on him. They could not have taken him, if he had not surrendered himself, and been <hi type="italic">delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>. He who said concerning his anointed servants, <hi type="italic">Touch them not,</hi> and <hi type="italic">do them no harm</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.14-Ps.105.15">Ps. cv. 14, 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">spared not his anointed Son, but delivered him up for us all;</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">gave his strength into captivity, his glory into the enemies' hands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.61">Ps. lxxviii. 61</reference>. See what was the complaint of Job (<reference osisRef="Job.16.11">ch. xvi. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">God hath delivered me to the ungodly,</hi> and apply that and other passages in that book of Job as a type of Christ. <div eID="gen23951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23952" type="x-p"/> Our Lord Jesus was made a prisoner, because he would in all things be treated as a malefactor, punished for our crime, and as a surety under arrest for our debt. The yoke of our transgressions was bound by the Father's hand upon the neck of the Lord Jesus, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.14">Lam. i. 14</reference>. He became a prisoner, that he might set us at liberty; for he said, <hi type="italic">If ye seek me, let these go their way</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.18.8">John xviii. 8</reference>); and those are free indeed, whom he makes so. <div eID="gen23952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23953" type="x-p"/> 3. How Peter fought for Christ, and was checked for his pains. It is here only said to be <hi type="italic">one of them that were with Jesus in the garden;</hi> but <reference osisRef="John.18.10">John xviii. 10</reference>, we are told that it was Peter who signalized himself upon this occasion. Observe, <div eID="gen23953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23954" type="x-p"/> (1.) Peter's rashness (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.51">v. 51</reference>); He <hi type="italic">drew his sword.</hi> They had but two swords among them all (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.38">Luke xxii. 38</reference>), and one of them, it seems, fell to Peter's share; and now he thought it was time to draw it, and he laid about him as if he would have done some great matter; but all the execution he did was the cutting off an ear from a servant of the High Priest; designing, it is likely, to cleave him down the head, because he saw him more forward than the rest in laying hands on Christ, he missed his blow. But if he would be striking, in my mind he should rather have aimed at Judas, and have marked him for a rogue. Peter had talked much of what he would do for his Master, he would <hi type="italic">lay down his life for him;</hi> yea, that he would; and now he would be as good as his word, and venture his life to rescue his Master: and thus far was commendable, that he had a great <hi type="italic">zeal</hi> for Christ, and his honour and safety; but it was not <hi type="italic">according to knowledge,</hi> nor guided by discretion; for [1.] He did it without warrant; some of the disciples asked indeed, <hi type="italic">Shall we smite with the sword?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.49">Luke xxii. 49</reference>) But Peter struck before they had an answer. We must see not only our cause good, but our call clear, before we draw the sword; we must show by what authority we do it, and who gave us that authority. [2.] He indiscreetly exposed himself and his fellow-disciples to the rage of the multitude; for what could they with two swords do against a band of men? <div eID="gen23954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23955" type="x-p"/> (2.) The rebuke which our Lord Jesus gave him (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.52">v. 52</reference>); <hi type="italic">Put up again thy sword into its place.</hi> He does not command the officers and soldiers to put up their swords that were drawn against him, he left them to the judgment of God, who judges them that are without; but he commands Peter to put up his sword, does not chide him indeed for what he had done, because done out of good will, but stops the progress of his arms, and provides that it should not be drawn into a precedent. Christ's errand into the world was to make peace. Note, <hi type="italic">The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but spiritual;</hi> and Christ's ministers, though they are his soldiers, do not <hi type="italic">war after the flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.3-2Cor.10.4">2 Cor. x. 3, 4</reference>. Not that the law of Christ overthrows either the law of nature of the law of nations, as far as those warrant subjects to stand up in defence of their civil rights and liberties, and their religion, when it is incorporated with them; but it provides for the preservation of public peace and order, by forbidding private persons, <hi type="italic">qua tales—as such,</hi> to resist the powers that are; nay, we have a general precept that we <hi type="italic">resist not evil</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.39">ch. v. 39</reference>), nor will Christ have his ministers propagate his religion by force of arms, <hi type="italic">Religio cogi non potest; et defendenda non occidendo, sed moriendo—Religion cannot be forced; and it should be defended, not by killing, but by dying.</hi> Lactantii Institut. As Christ forbade his disciples the sword of justice (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.25-Matt.20.26">ch. xx. 25, 26</reference>), so here the sword of war. Christ bade Peter put up his sword, and never bade him draw it again; yet that which Peter is here blamed for is his doing it unseasonably; the hour was come for Christ to suffer and die, he knew Peter knew it, the <hi type="italic">sword of the Lord was drawn against him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.7">Zech. xiii. 7</reference>), and for Peter to draw his sword for him, was like, <hi type="italic">Master, spare thyself.</hi> <div eID="gen23955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23956" type="x-p"/> Three reasons Christ give to Peter for this rebuke: <div eID="gen23956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23957" type="x-p"/> [1.] His drawing the sword would be dangerous to himself and to his fellow-disciples; <hi type="italic">They that take the sword, shall perish with the sword;</hi> they that use violence, fall by violence; and men hasten and increase their own troubles by blustering bloody methods of self-defence. They that take the sword before it is given them, that use it without warrant or call, expose themselves to the sword of war, or public justice. Had it not been for the special care and providence of the Lord Jesus, Peter and the rest of them had, for aught I know, been cut in pieces immediately. Grotius gives another, and a probable sense of this blow, making those that take the sword to be, not Peter, but the officers and soldiers that come with swords <hi type="italic">to take Christ;</hi> They shall <hi type="italic">perish with the sword.</hi> "Peter, thou needest not draw they sword to punish them. God will certainly, shortly, and severely, reckon with them." They took the Roman sword to seize Christ with, and by the Roman sword, not long after, they and their place and nation were destroyed. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> we must not <hi type="italic">avenge ourselves,</hi> because <hi type="italic">God will repay</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.19">Rom. xii. 19</reference>); and therefore we must suffer with faith and patience, because persecutors will be paid in their own coin. See <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Rev. xiii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen23957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23958" type="x-p"/> [2.] It was needless for him to draw his sword in defence of his Master, who, if he pleased, could summon into his service all the hosts of heaven (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.53">v. 53</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall send</hi> from heaven effectual succours? Peter, if I would put by these sufferings, I could easily do it without thy hand or thy sword." Note, God has no need of us, of our services, much less of our sins, to bring about his purposes; and it argues our distrust and disbelief of the power of Christ, when we go out of the way of our duty to serve his interests. God can do his work without us; if we look into the heavens, and see how he is attended there, we may easily infer, that, <hi type="italic">though we be righteous,</hi> he is not beholden to us, <reference osisRef="Job.35.5">Job xxxv. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.35.7">7</reference>. Though Christ was crucified through weakness, it was a voluntary weakness; he submitted to death, not because he could not, but because he would not contend with it. This takes off the offence of the cross, and proves Christ crucified the power of God; even now in the depth of his sufferings he could call in the aid of legions of angels. <hi type="italic">Now,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">arti</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">yet;</hi> "Though the business is so far gone, I could yet with a word speaking turn the scale." Christ here lets us know, <div eID="gen23958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23959" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What a great interest he had in his Father; <hi type="italic">I can pray to my Father, and he will send me help from the sanctuary.</hi> I can <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">parakalesai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">demand of my Father these succours.</hi> Christ prayed <hi type="italic">as one having authority.</hi> Note, It is a great comfort to God's people, when they are surrounded with enemies on all hands, that they have a way open heavenward; if they can do nothing else, they can pray to him that can do every thing. And they who are much in prayer at other times, have most comfort in praying when troublesome times come. Observe, Christ saith, not only that God could send him such a number of angels, but that, if he insisted upon it, he would do it. Though he had undertaken the work of our redemption, yet, if he had desired to be released, it should seem by this that the Father would not have held him to it. He might yet have gone out free from the service, but he loved it, and would not; so that it was only with the cords of his own love that he was bound to the altar. <div eID="gen23959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23960" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> What a great interest he had in the heavenly hosts; <hi type="italic">He shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels,</hi> amounting to above seventy-two thousand. Observe here, 1. There is an <hi type="italic">innumerable company of angels,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">Heb. xii. 2</reference>. A detachment of more than twelve legions might be spared for our service, and yet there would be no miss of them about the throne. See <reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">Dan. vii. 10</reference>. They are marshalled in exact order, like the well-disciplined legions; not a confused multitude, but regular troops; all know their post, and observe the word of command. 2. This innumerable company of angels are all at the disposal of our heavenly Father, and do his pleasure, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.20-Ps.103.21">Ps. ciii. 20, 21</reference>. 3. These angelic hosts were ready to come in to the assistance of our Lord Jesus in his sufferings, if he had needed or desired it. See <reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">Heb. i. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.14">14</reference>. They would have been to him as they were to Elisha, <hi type="italic">chariots of fire, and horses of fire,</hi> not only to secure him, but to consume those that set upon him. 4. Our heavenly Father is to be eyed and acknowledged in all the services of the heavenly hosts; <hi type="italic">He shall give them me:</hi> therefore angels are not to be prayed to, but the Lord of the angels, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.11">Ps. xci. 11</reference>. 5. It is matter of comfort to all that wish well to the kingdom of Christ, that there is a world of angels always at the service of the Lord Jesus, that can do wonders. He that has the armies of heaven at his beck, can do what he pleases among the <hi type="italic">inhabitants of the earth;</hi> He shall <hi type="italic">presently</hi> give them me. See how ready his Father was to hear his prayer, and how ready the angels were to observe his orders; they are willing servants, winged messengers, they <hi type="italic">fly swiftly.</hi> This is very encouraging to those that have the honour of Christ, and the welfare of his church, much at heart. Think they that they have more care and concern for Christ and his church, than God and the holy angels have? <div eID="gen23960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23961" type="x-p"/> [3.] It was no time to make any defence at all, or to offer to put by the stroke; <hi type="italic">For how then shall the scripture be fulfilled, that thus it must be?</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.26.54">v. 54</reference>. It was written, that Christ should be <hi type="italic">led as a lamb to the slaughter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.7">Isa. liii. 7</reference>. Should he summon the angels to his assistance, he would not be led to the slaughter at all; should he permit his disciples to fight, he would not be led as a lamb quietly and without resistance; therefore he and his disciples must yield to the accomplishment of the predictions. Note, In all difficult cases, the word of God must be conclusive against our own counsels, and nothing must be done, nothing attempted, against the fulfilling of the scripture. If the easing of our pains, the breaking of our bonds, the saving of our lives, will not consist with the fulfilling of the scripture, we ought to say, "Let God's word and will take place, let his law be magnified and made honourable, whatever becomes of us." Thus Christ checked Peter, when he set up for his champion, and captain of his life-guard. <div eID="gen23961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23962" type="x-p"/> 4. We are next told how Christ argued the case with them that came to take him (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.55">v. 55</reference>); though he did not resist them, yet he did reason with them. Note, It will consist with Christian patience under our sufferings, calmly to expostulate with our enemies and persecutors, as David with Saul, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.14">1 Sam. xxiv. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.18">xxvi. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">Are ye come out,</hi> (1.) With rage and enmity, <hi type="italic">as against a thief,</hi> as if I were an enemy to the public safety, and deservedly suffered this? Thieves draw upon themselves the common odium; every one will lend a hand to stop a thief: and thus they fell upon Christ as the offscouring of all things. If he had been the plague of his country, he could not have been prosecuted with more heat and violence. (2.) With all this power and force, as against the worst of thieves, that dare the law, bid defiance to public justice, and add rebellion to their sin? You are come out as against a thief, with swords and staves, as if there were danger of resistance; whereas ye have <hi type="italic">killed the just One, and he doth not resist you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.6">Jam. v. 6</reference>. If he had not been willing to suffer, it was folly to <hi type="italic">come with swords and staves, for they could not conquer him;</hi> had he been minded to resist, he would have esteemed their iron as straw, and their swords and staves would have been as briars before a consuming fire; but, being willing to suffer, it was folly to come thus armed, for he would not contend with them. <div eID="gen23962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23963" type="x-p"/> He further expostulates with them, by reminding them how he had behaved himself hitherto toward them, and they toward him. [1.] Of his public appearance; <hi type="italic">I sat daily with you in the temple teaching.</hi> And, [2.] Of their public connivance; <hi type="italic">Ye laid no hold on me.</hi> How comes then this change? They were very unreasonable, in treating him as they did. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He had given them no occasion to look upon him as a thief, for he had taught in the temple. And such were the matter, and such the manner of his teaching, that he was manifested in the consciences of all that heard him, not to be a bad man. Such gracious words as came from his mouth, were not the words of a thief, nor of one that had a devil. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Nor had he given them occasion to look upon him as one that absconded, or fled from justice, that they should come in the night to seize him; if they had any thing to say to him, they might find him every day in the temple, ready to answer all challenges, all charges, and there they might do as they pleased with him; for the chief priests had the custody of the temple, and the command of the guards about it; but to come upon him thus clandestinely, in the place of his retirement, was base and cowardly. Thus the greatest hero may be villainously assassinated in a corner, by one that in open field would tremble to look him in the face. <div eID="gen23963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23964" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">But all this was done</hi> (so it follows, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.56">v. 56</reference>) <hi type="italic">that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.</hi> It is hard to say, whether these are the words of the sacred historian, as a comment upon this story, and a direction to the Christian reader to compare it with the scriptures of the Old Testament, which pointed at it; or, whether they are the words of Christ himself, as a reason why, though he could not but resent this base treatment, he yet submitted to it, that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled, to which he had just now referred himself, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.54">v. 54</reference>. Note, The scriptures are in the fulfilling every day; and all those scriptures which speak of the Messiah, had their full accomplishment in our Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen23964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23965" type="x-p"/> 5. How he was, in the midst of this distress, shamefully deserted by his disciples; <hi type="italic">They all forsook him, and fled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.26.56">v. 56</reference>. <div eID="gen23965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23966" type="x-p"/> (1.) This was their sin; and it was a great sin for them who had left all to follow him, now to leave him for they knew not what. There was unkindness in it, considering the relation they stood in to him, the favours they had received from him, and the melancholy circumstances he was now in. There was unfaithfulness in it, for they had solemnly promised to adhere to him, and never to forsake him. He had indented for their safe conduct (<reference osisRef="John.18.8">John xviii. 8</reference>); yet they could not rely upon that, but shifted for themselves by an inglorious flight. What folly was this, for fear of death to flee from him whom they themselves knew and had acknowledged to be the <hi type="italic">Fountain of life?</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.67-John.6.68">John vi. 67, 68</reference>. <hi type="italic">Lord, what is man!</hi> <div eID="gen23966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23967" type="x-p"/> (2.) It was a part of Christ's suffering, it added affliction to his bonds, to be thus deserted, as it did to Job (<reference osisRef="Job.19.13">ch. xix. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">He hath put my brethren far from me;</hi> and to David (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.11">Ps. xxxviii. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">Lovers and friends stand aloof from my sore.</hi> They should have staid with him, to minister to him, to countenance him, and, if need were, to be witnesses for him at his trial; but they treacherously deserted him, as, at St. Paul's <hi type="italic">first answer, no man stood with him.</hi> But there was a mystery in this. [1.] Christ, as a sacrifice for sins, stood thus abandoned. The deer that by the keeper's arrow is marked out to be hunted and run down, is immediately deserted by the whole herd. In this he was made a curse for us, being left as one separated to evil. [2.] Christ, as the Saviour of souls, stood thus alone; as he needed not, so he had not the assistance of any other in working out our salvation; he bore all, and did all himself. He <hi type="italic">trod the wine-press alone,</hi> and when there was <hi type="italic">none to uphold,</hi> then <hi type="italic">his own arm wrought salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.63.3">Isa. lxiii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">5</reference>. So <hi type="italic">the Lord alone did lead his Israel,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">stand still, and only see this great salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.12">Deut. xxxii. 12</reference>.
entries.c7676d34aa4b0f62ca32c8e340ad6a6768285f68: <div eID="gen23967" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ in the High Priest's Palace.</title> <div sID="gen23968" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">57</hi> And they that had laid hold on Jesus led <hi type="italic">him</hi> away to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders were assembled. <hi type="super">58</hi> But Peter followed him afar off unto the high priest's palace, and went in, and sat with the servants, to see the end. <hi type="super">59</hi> Now the chief priests, and elders, and all the council, sought false witness against Jesus, to put him to death; <hi type="super">60</hi> But found none: yea, though many false witnesses came, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> found they none. At the last came two false witnesses, <hi type="super">61</hi> And said, This <hi type="italic">fellow</hi> said, I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to build it in three days. 62 And the high priest arose, and said unto him, Answerest thou nothing? what <hi type="italic">is it which</hi> these witness against thee? 63 But Jesus held his peace. And the high priest answered and said unto him, I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God. <hi type="super">64</hi> Jesus saith unto him, Thou hast said: nevertheless I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven. <hi type="super">65</hi> Then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy; what further need have we of witnesses? behold, now ye have heard his blasphemy. <hi type="super">66</hi> What think ye? They answered and said, He is guilty of death. <hi type="super">67</hi> Then did they spit in his face, and buffeted him; and others smote <hi type="italic">him</hi> with the palms of their hands, <hi type="super">68</hi> Saying, Prophesy unto us, thou Christ, Who is he that smote thee? <div eID="gen23968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23969" type="x-p"/> We have here the arraignment of our Lord Jesus in the ecclesiastical court, before the great sanhedrim. Observe, <div eID="gen23969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23970" type="x-p"/> I. The sitting of the court; the scribes and the elders were assembled, though it was in the dead time of the night, when other people were fast asleep in their beds; yet, to gratify their malice against Christ, they denied themselves that natural rest, and sat up all night, to be ready to fall upon the prey which Judas and his men, they hoped, would <hi type="italic">seize.</hi> <div eID="gen23970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23971" type="x-p"/> See, 1. Who they were, that were assembled; the <hi type="italic">scribes,</hi> the principal teachers, and <hi type="italic">elders,</hi> the principal rulers, of the Jewish church: these were the most bitter enemies to Christ our great teacher and ruler, on whom therefore they had a jealous eye, as one that eclipsed them; perhaps some of these scribes and elders were not so malicious at Christ as some others of them were; yet, in concurrence with the rest, they made themselves guilty. Now the scripture was fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">Ps. xxii. 16</reference>); <hi type="italic">The assembly of the wicked have enclosed me.</hi> Jeremiah complains of an assembly of treacherous men; and David of his enemies <hi type="italic">gathering themselves together against him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.35.15">Ps. xxxv. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen23971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23972" type="x-p"/> 2. Where they were assembled; <hi type="italic">in the palace of Caiaphas the High Priest;</hi> there they assembled two days before, to lay the plot (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.3">v. 3</reference>), and there they now convened again, to prosecute it. The <hi type="italic">High Priest</hi> was <hi type="italic">Ab-beth-din—the father of the house of judgment,</hi> but he is now the patron of wickedness; his house should have been the sanctuary of oppressed innocency, but it is become the throne of iniquity; and no wonder, when even God's house of prayer was made a den of thieves. <div eID="gen23972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23973" type="x-p"/> II. The setting of the prisoner to the bar; they that had <hi type="italic">laid hold on Jesus, led him away,</hi> hurried him, no doubt, with violence, led him as a trophy of their victory, led him as a victim to the altar; he was brought into Jerusalem through that which was called the <hi type="italic">sheep-gate,</hi> for that was the way into town from the mount of Olives; and it was so called because the sheep appointed for sacrifice were brought that way to the temple; very fitly therefore is Christ led that way, who is the Lamb of God, that takes away the sin of the world. Christ was led first to the High Priest, for by the law all sacrifices were to be first <hi type="italic">presented to the priest, and delivered into his hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.17.5">Lev. xvii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen23973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23974" type="x-p"/> III. The cowardice and faint-heartedness of Peter (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.58">v. 58</reference>); <hi type="italic">But Peter followed afar off.</hi> This comes in here, with an eye to the following story of his denying him. He forsook him as the rest did, when he was seized, and what is here said of his following him is easily reconcilable with his forsaking him; such following was no better than forsaking him; for, <div eID="gen23974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23975" type="x-p"/> 1. He followed him, but it was <hi type="italic">afar off.</hi> Some sparks of love and concern for his Master there were in his breast, and therefore he followed him; but fear and concern for his own safety prevailed, and therefore he followed afar off. Note, It looks ill, and bodes worse, when those that are willing to be Christ's disciples, are not willing to be known to be so. Here began Peter's denying him; for to follow him afar off, is by little and little to go back from him. There is danger in drawing back, nay, in looking back. <div eID="gen23975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23976" type="x-p"/> 2. He followed him, but he <hi type="italic">went in, and sat with the servants.</hi> He should have gone up to the court, and attended on his Master, and appeared for him; but he went in where there was a good fire, and sat with the servants, not to silence their reproaches, but to screen himself. It was presumption in Peter thus to thrust himself into temptation; he that does so, throws himself out of God's protection. Christ had told Peter that he could not follow him now, and had particularly warned him of his danger <hi type="italic">this night;</hi> and yet he would venture into the midst of this wicked crew. It helped David to walk in his integrity, that he <hi type="italic">hated the congregation of evil doers, and would not sit with the wicked.</hi> <div eID="gen23976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23977" type="x-p"/> 3. He followed him, but it was only <hi type="italic">to see the end,</hi> led more by his curiosity than by his conscience; he attended as an idle spectator rather than as a disciple, a person concerned. He should have gone in, to do Christ some service, or to get some wisdom and grace to himself, by observing Christ's behaviour under his sufferings: but he went in, only to look about him; it is not unlikely that Peter went in, expecting that Christ would have made his escape miraculously out of the hands of his persecutors; that, having so lately struck them down, who came to seize him, he would now have struck them dead, who sat to judge him; and this he had a mind to see: if so, it was folly for him to think of seeing any other end than what Christ had foretold, that he should be put to death. Note, It is more our concern to prepare for the end, whatever it may be, than curiously to enquire what the end will be. The event is God's, but the duty is ours. <div eID="gen23977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23978" type="x-p"/> IV. The trial of our Lord Jesus in this court. <div eID="gen23978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23979" type="x-p"/> 1. They examined witnesses against him, though they were resolved, right or wrong, to condemn him; yet, to put the better colour upon it, they would produce evidence against him. The crimes properly cognizable in their court, were, false doctrine and blasphemy; these they endeavoured to prove upon him. And observe here, <div eID="gen23979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23980" type="x-p"/> (1.) Their search for proof; <hi type="italic">They sought false witness against him;</hi> they had seized him, bound him, abused him, and after all have to seek for something to lay to his charge, and can show no cause for his commitment. They tried if any of them could allege seemingly from their own knowledge any thing against him; and suggested one calumny and then another, which, if true, might touch his life. Thus <hi type="italic">evil men dig up mischief,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.16.27">Prov. xvi. 27</reference>. Here they trod in the steps of their predecessors, who <hi type="italic">devised devices against Jeremiah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.18.18">Jer. xviii. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.20.10">xx. 10</reference>. They made proclamation, that, if any one could give information against the prisoner at the bar, they were ready to receive it, and presently many bore false witness against him (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.60">v. 60</reference>); for is <hi type="italic">a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked,</hi> and will carry false stories to him, <reference osisRef="Prov.29.12">Prov. xxix. 12</reference>. This is an evil often seen under the sun, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.5">Eccl. x. 5</reference>. If Naboth must be taken off, there are sons of Belial to swear against him. <div eID="gen23980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23981" type="x-p"/> (2.) Their success in this search; in several attempts they were baffled, they sought false testimonies among themselves, others came in to help them, and yet they found none; they could make nothing of it, could not take the evidence together, or give it any colour of truth or consistency with itself, no, not they themselves being judges. The matters alleged were such palpable lies, as carried their own confutation along with them. This redounded much to the honour of Christ now, when they were loading him with disgrace. <div eID="gen23981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23982" type="x-p"/> But at last they met with <hi type="italic">two</hi> witnesses, who, it seems, agreed in their evidence, and therefore were hearkened to, in hopes that now the point was gained. The words they swore against him, were, that he should say, <hi type="italic">I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to build it in three days,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.26.61">v. 61</reference>. Now by this they designed to accuse him, [1.] As an enemy to the temple, and one that sought for the destruction of it, which they could not bear to hear of; for they valued themselves by <hi type="italic">the temple of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jer. vii. 4</reference>), and, when they abandoned other idols, made a perfect idol of that. Stephen was accused for <hi type="italic">speaking against this holy place,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.6.13-Acts.6.14">Acts vi. 13, 14</reference>. [2.] As one that dealt in witchcraft, or some such unlawful arts, by the help of which he could rear such a building in three days: they had often suggested that he was in league with Beelzebub. Now, as to this, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The words were mis-recited; he said, <hi type="italic">Destroy ye this temple</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.2.19">John ii. 19</reference>), plainly intimating that he spoke of a temple which his enemies would seek to destroy; they come, and swear that he said, <hi type="italic">I am able to destroy</hi> this temple, as if the design against it were his. He said, <hi type="italic">In Three days I will raise it up</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">egero auton</hi></hi>, a word properly used of a living temple; <hi type="italic">I will raise it to life.</hi> They come, and swear that he said, <hi type="italic">I am able,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">oikodomesai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">to build it;</hi> which is properly used of a house temple. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The words were misunderstood; <hi type="italic">he spoke of the temple of his body</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.2.21">John ii. 21</reference>), and perhaps when he said, <hi type="italic">this temple,</hi> pointed to, or laid his hand upon, his own body; but they swore that he said the <hi type="italic">temple of God,</hi> meaning this holy place. Note, There have been, and still are, such as <hi type="italic">wrest</hi> the sayings of Christ <hi type="italic">to their own destruction,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.16">2 Pet. iii. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Make the worst they could of it, it was no capital crime, even by their own law; if it had been, no question but he had been prosecuted for it, when he spoke the words in a public discourse some years ago; nay, the words were capable of a laudable construction, and such as bespoke a kindness for the temple; if it were destroyed, he would exert himself to the utmost to rebuild it. But any thing that looked criminal, would serve to give colour to their malicious prosecution. Now the scriptures were fulfilled, which said, <hi type="italic">False witnesses are risen up against me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.12">Ps. xxvii. 12</reference>); and see <reference osisRef="Ps.35.11">Ps. xxxv. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">Though I have redeemed them, yet they have spoken lies against me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.7.13">Hos. vii. 13</reference>. We stand justly accused, the law <hi type="italic">accuseth us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.27.26">Deut. xxvii. 26</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.45">John v. 45</reference>. Satan and our own consciences accuse us, <reference osisRef="1John.3.20">1 John iii. 20</reference>. The creatures cry out against us. Now, to discharge us from all these just accusations, our Lord Jesus submitted to this, to be unjustly and falsely accused, that in the virtue of his sufferings we may be enabled to triumph over all challenges; <hi type="italic">Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect?</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.33-Rom.8.34">Rom. viii. 33, 34</reference>.
