He was accused, that he might not be condemned; and if at any time we suffer thus, have all manner of evil, not only said, but <hi type="italic">sworn, against us falsely,</hi> let us remember that we cannot expect to fare better than our Master. <div eID="gen23982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23983" type="x-p"/> (3.) Christ's silence under all these accusations, to the amazement of the court, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.62">v. 62</reference>. The High Priest, the judge of the court, arose in some heat, and said, "<hi type="italic">Answerest thou nothing?</hi> Come, you the prisoner at the bar; you hear what is sworn against you, what have you now to say for yourself? What defence can you make? Or what plea have you to offer in answer to this charge?" <hi type="italic">But Jesus held his peace</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.63">v. 63</reference>), not as one sullen, or as one self-condemned, or as one astonished and in confusion; not because he wanted something to say, or knew not how to say it, but that the scripture might be fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.7">Isa. liii. 7</reference>); <hi type="italic">As the sheep is dumb before the shearer,</hi> and before the butcher, <hi type="italic">so he opened not his mouth;</hi> and that he might be the Son of David, who, when his enemies spoke mischievous things against him, was <hi type="italic">as a deaf man that heard not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.12-Ps.38.14">Ps. xxxviii. 12-14</reference>. He was silent, because <hi type="italic">his hour was come;</hi> he would not deny the charge, because he was willing to submit to the sentence; otherwise, he could as easily have put them to silence and shame now, as he had done many a time before. If God had entered into judgment with us, we had been <hi type="italic">speechless</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.12">ch. xxii. 12</reference>), not able to <hi type="italic">answer for one of a thousand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.9.3">Job ix. 3</reference>. Therefore, when Christ was <hi type="italic">made sin for us,</hi> he was silent, and left it to his blood to speak, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.24">Heb. xii. 24</reference>. He stood mute at this bar, that we might have something to say at God's bar. <div eID="gen23983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23984" type="x-p"/> Well, this way will not do; <hi type="italic">ali&#226; aggrediendum est vi&#226;—recourse must be had to some other expedient.</hi> <div eID="gen23984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23985" type="x-p"/> 2. They examined our Lord Jesus himself upon an oath like that <hi type="italic">ex officio;</hi> and, since they could not accuse him, they will try, contrary to the law of equity, to make him accuse himself. <div eID="gen23985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23986" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is the interrogatory put to him by the High Priest. <div eID="gen23986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23987" type="x-p"/> Observe, [1.] The question itself; <hi type="italic">Whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God?</hi> That is, Whether thou pretend to be so? For they will by no means admit it into consideration, whether he be really so or no; though the Messiah was to <hi type="italic">be the Consolation of Israel,</hi> and glorious things were spoken concerning him in the Old Testament, yet so strangely besotted were they with a jealousy of any thing that threatened their exorbitant power and grandeur, that they would never enter into the examination of the matter, whether Jesus was the Messiah or no; never once put the case, suppose he should be so; they only wished him to confess that he called himself so, that they might on that indict him as a deceiver. What will not pride and malice carry men to? <div eID="gen23987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23988" type="x-p"/> [2.] The solemnity of the proposal of it; <hi type="italic">I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us.</hi> Not that he had any regard to the living God, but took his name in vain; only thus he hoped to gain his point with our Lord Jesus; "If thou hast any value for the blessed name of God, and reverence for his Majesty, tell us this." If he should refuse to answer when he was thus adjured, they would charge him with contempt of the blessed name of God. Thus the persecutors of good men often take advantage against them by their consciences, as Daniel's enemies did against him in the matter of his God. <div eID="gen23988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23989" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ's answer to this interrogatory (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.64">v. 64</reference>), in which, <div eID="gen23989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23990" type="x-p"/> [1.] He owns himself to be <hi type="italic">The Christ the Son of God. Thou hast said;</hi> that is, "It is as thou hast said;" for in St. Mark it is, <hi type="italic">I am.</hi> Hitherto, he seldom professed himself expressly to be the Christ, the Son of God; the tenour of his doctrine bespoke it, and his miracles proved it: but now he would not omit to make a confession of it, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because that would have looked like a disowning of that truth which he came into the world to bear witness to. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It would have looked like declining his sufferings, when he knew the acknowledgment of this would give his enemies all the advantage they desired against him. He thus confessed himself, for example and encouragement to his followers, when they are called to it, to <hi type="italic">confess him before men,</hi> whatever hazards they run by it. And according to this pattern the martyrs readily confessed themselves Christians, though they knew they must die for it, as the martyrs at Thebais, <hi type="italic">Euseb. Hist.</hi> 50.8, 100.9. That Christ answered out of a regard to the adjuration which Caiaphas had profanely used by the <hi type="italic">living God,</hi> I cannot think, any more than that he had any regard to the like adjuration in the devil's mouth, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.7">Mark v. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen23990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23991" type="x-p"/> [2.] He refers himself, for the proof of this, to his second coming, and indeed to his whole estate of exaltation. It is probable that they looked upon him with a scornful disdainful smile, when he said, "<hi type="italic">I am;</hi>" "A likely fellow," thought they, "to be the Messiah, who is expected to come in so much pomp and power;" and to that this <hi type="italic">nevertheless</hi> refers. "Though now you see me in this low and abject state, and think it a ridiculous thing for me to call myself the Messiah, <hi type="italic">nevertheless</hi> the day is coming when I shall appear otherwise." <hi type="italic">Hereafter,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ap arti</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">&#224; modo—shortly;</hi> for his exaltation began in a few days; now shortly his kingdom began to be set up; and <hi type="italic">hereafter ye shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, to judge the world;</hi> of which his coming shortly to judge and destroy the Jewish nation would be a type and earnest. Note, The terrors of the judgment-day will be a sensible conviction to the most obstinate infidelity, not in order to conversion (that will be then too late), but in order to an eternal confusion. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Whom they should see; <hi type="italic">the Son of man.</hi> Having owned himself the Son of God, even now in his estate of humiliation, he speaks of himself as the Son of man, even in his estate of exaltation; for he had these two distinct natures in one person. The incarnation of Christ has made him Son of God and Son of man; for he is <hi type="italic">Immanuel,</hi> God with us. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> In what posture they should see him; 1. <hi type="italic">Sitting on the right hand of power,</hi> according to the prophecy of the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Ps. cx. 1</reference>); <hi type="italic">Sit thou at my right hand;</hi> which denotes both the dignity and the dominion he is exalted to. Though now he stood at the bar, they should shortly see him sit on the throne. 2. <hi type="italic">Coming in the clouds of heaven;</hi> this refers to another prophecy concerning the <hi type="italic">Son of man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.13-Dan.7.14">Dan. vii. 13, 14</reference>), which is applied to Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.33">Luke i. 33</reference>), when he came to destroy Jerusalem; so terrible was the judgment, and so sensible the indications of the wrath of the Lamb in it, that it might be called <hi type="italic">a visible appearance of Christ;</hi> but doubtless it has reference to the general judgment; to this day he appeals, and summons them to an appearance, then and there to answer for what they are now doing. He had spoken of this day to his disciples, awhile ago, for their comfort, and had bid them <hi type="italic">lift up their heads</hi> for joy in the prospect of it, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.27-Luke.21.28">Luke xxi. 27, 28</reference>. Now he speaks of it to his enemies, for their terror; for nothing is more comfortable to the righteous, nor more terrible to the wicked, than Christ's judging the world at the last day. <div eID="gen23991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23992" type="x-p"/> V. His conviction upon this trial; <hi type="italic">The High Priest rent his clothes,</hi> according to the custom of the Jews, when they heard or saw any thing done or said, which they looked upon to be a reproach to God; as <reference osisRef="Isa.36.22">Isa. xxxvi. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.1">xxxvii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.14">Acts xiv. 14</reference>. Caiaphas would be thought extremely tender of the glory of God (<hi type="italic">Come, see his zeal for the Lord of hosts</hi>); but, while he pretended an abhorrence of blasphemy, he was himself the greatest blasphemer; he now forgot the law which forbade the High Priest in any case to rend his clothes, unless we will suppose this an excepted case. <div eID="gen23992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23993" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. The crime he was found guilty of; <hi type="italic">blasphemy. He hath spoken blasphemy;</hi> that is, he hath spoken reproachfully of the living God; that is the notion we have of blasphemy; because we by sin had reproached the Lord, therefore Christ, when <hi type="italic">he was made Sin for us,</hi> was condemned as a blasphemer for the truth he told them. <div eID="gen23993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23994" type="x-p"/> 2. The evidence upon which they found him guilty; <hi type="italic">Ye have heard the blasphemy;</hi> why should we trouble ourselves to examine <hi type="italic">witnesses</hi> any further? He owned the fact, that he did profess himself the <hi type="italic">Son of God;</hi> and then they made blasphemy of it, and convicted him upon his confession. The High Priest triumphs in the success of the snare he had laid; "Now I think I have done his business for him." <hi type="italic">Aha, so would we have it.</hi> Thus was he <hi type="italic">judged out of his own mouth</hi> at their bar, because we were liable to be so judged at God's bar. There is no need of witnesses against us; our own consciences are against us instead of a thousand witnesses. <div eID="gen23994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23995" type="x-p"/> VI. His sentence passed, upon this conviction, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.66">v. 66</reference>. <div eID="gen23995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23996" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. Caiaphas's appeal to the bench; <hi type="italic">What think ye?</hi> See his base hypocrisy and partiality; when he had already prejudged the cause, and pronounced him a blasphemer, then, as if he were willing to be advised, he asks the judgment of his brethren; but hide malice ever so cunningly under the robe of justice, some way or other it will break out. If he would have dealt fairly, he should have collected the votes of the bench <hi type="italic">seriatim—in order,</hi> and begun with the junior, and delivered his own opinion last; but he knew that by the authority of his place he could sway the rest, and therefore declares his judgment, and presumes they are all of his mind; he takes the crime, with regard to Christ, <hi type="italic">pro confesso—as a crime confessed;</hi> and the judgment, with regard to the court, <hi type="italic">pro concesso—as a judgment agreed to.</hi> <div eID="gen23996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23997" type="x-p"/> 2. Their concurrence with him; they said, <hi type="italic">He is guilty of death;</hi> perhaps they did not all concur: it is certain that Joseph of Arimathea, if he was present, dissented (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.51">Luke xxiii. 51</reference>); so did Nicodemus, and, it is likely, others with them; however, the majority carried it that way; but, perhaps, this being an extraordinary council, or cabal rather, none had notice to be present but such as they knew would concur, and so it might be voted <hi type="italic">nemine contradicente—unanimously.</hi> The judgment was, "<hi type="italic">He is guilty of death;</hi> by the law he deserves to die." Though they had not power now to put any man to death, yet by such a judgment as this they made a man an <hi type="italic">outlaw</hi> among his people (<hi type="italic">qui caput gerit lupinum—he carries a wolf's head;</hi> so our old law describes an outlaw), and so exposed him to the fury either of a popular tumult, as Stephen was, or to be clamoured against before the governor, as Christ was. Thus was the Lord of life condemned to die, that through him there may be <hi type="italic">no condemnation to us.</hi> <div eID="gen23997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23998" type="x-p"/> VII. The abuses and indignities done to him after sentence passed (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.67-Matt.26.68">v. 67, 68</reference>); <hi type="italic">Then,</hi> when he was found guilty, they <hi type="italic">spat in his face.</hi> Because they had not power to put him to death, and could not be sure that they should prevail with the governor to be their executioner, they would do him all the mischief they could, now that they had him in their hands. Condemned prisoners are taken under the special protection of the law, which they are to make satisfaction to, and by all civilized nations have been treated with tenderness; sufficient is this punishment. But when they had passed sentence upon our Lord Jesus, he was treated as if hell had broken loose upon him, as if he were not only <hi type="italic">worthy of death,</hi> but as if that were too good for him, and he were unworthy of the compassion shown to the worst malefactors. Thus <hi type="italic">he was made a curse for us.</hi> But who were they that were thus barbarous? It should seem, the very same that had passed sentence upon him. <hi type="italic">They said, He is guilty of death, and then did they spit in his face.</hi> The priests began, and then no wonder if the servants, who would do any thing to make sport to themselves, and curry favour with their wicked masters, carried on the humour. See how they abused him. <div eID="gen23998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23999" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">They spat in his face.</hi> Thus the scripture was fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">Isa. l. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">He hid not his face from shame and spitting.</hi> Job complained of this indignity done to him, and herein was a type of Christ (<reference osisRef="Job.31.10">Job xxxi. 10</reference>); <hi type="italic">They spare not to spit in my face.</hi> It is an expression of the greatest contempt and indignation possible; looking upon him as more despicable than the very ground they spit upon. When Miriam was under the leprosy, it was looked upon as a disgrace to her, like that of <hi type="italic">her father spitting in her face,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.12.14">Num. xii. 14</reference>. He that refused to raise up seed to his brother, was to undergo this dishonour, <reference osisRef="Deut.25.9">Deut. xxv. 9</reference>. Yet Christ, when he was repairing the decays of the great family of mankind, submitted to it. That face which was <hi type="italic">fairer than the children of men,</hi> which was <hi type="italic">white and ruddy,</hi> and which angels reverence, was thus filthily abused by the basest and vilest of the children of men. Thus was confusion poured upon his face, that ours might not be filled with everlasting shame and contempt. They who now profane his blessed name, abuse his word, and hate his image in his sanctified ones; what do they better than spit in his face? They would do that, if it were in their reach. <div eID="gen23999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24000" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">They buffeted him, and smote him with the palms of their hands.</hi> This added pain to the shame, for both came in with sin. Now the scripture was fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">Isa. l. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">I gave my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair; and</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.30">Lam. iii. 30</reference>), <hi type="italic">He giveth his cheek to him that smiteth him; he is filled with reproach,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">keepeth silence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.28">v. 28</reference>); and (<reference osisRef="Mic.5.1">Mic. v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">They shall smite the Judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek;</hi> here the margin reads it, <hi type="italic">They smote him with rods;</hi> for so <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">errapisan</hi></hi> signifies, and this he submitted to. <div eID="gen24000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24001" type="x-p"/> 3. They challenged him to tell who struck him, having first blindfolded him; <hi type="italic">Prophesy unto us, thou Christ, who is he that smote thee?</hi> (1.) They made sport of him, as the Philistines did with Samson; it is grievous to those that are in misery, for people to make merry <hi type="italic">about</hi> them, but much more to make merry <hi type="italic">with</hi> them and their misery. Here was an instance of the greatest depravity and degeneracy of the human nature that could be, to show that there was need of a religion that should recover men to humanity. (2.) They made sport with his prophetical office. They had heard him called a <hi type="italic">prophet,</hi> and that he was famed for wonderful discoveries; this they upbraided him with, and pretended to make a trial of; as if the divine omniscience must stoop to a piece of children's play. <hi type="italic">They</hi> put a like affront upon Christ, who profanely jest with the scripture, and make themselves merry with holy things; like Belshazzar's revels in the temple bowls.
entries.bcbda22792c624cd651c25837c342373371ad6c7: <div eID="gen24001" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Denied by Peter.</title> <div sID="gen24002" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">69</hi> Now Peter sat without in the palace: and a damsel came unto him, saying, Thou also wast with Jesus of Galilee. 70 But he denied before <hi type="italic">them</hi> all, saying, I know not what thou sayest. <hi type="super">71</hi> And when he was gone out into the porch, another <hi type="italic">maid</hi> saw him, and said unto them that were there, This <hi type="italic">fellow</hi> was also with Jesus of Nazareth. <hi type="super">72</hi> And again he denied with an oath, I do not know the man. <hi type="super">73</hi> And after a while came unto <hi type="italic">him</hi> they that stood by, and said to Peter, Surely thou also art <hi type="italic">one</hi> of them; for thy speech bewrayeth thee. <hi type="super">74</hi> Then began he to curse and to swear, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> I know not the man. And immediately the cock crew. <hi type="super">75</hi> And Peter remembered the word of Jesus, which said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And he went out, and wept bitterly. <div eID="gen24002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24003" type="x-p"/> We have here the story of Peter's denying his Master, and it comes in as a part of Christ's sufferings. Our Lord Jesus was now in the High Priest's hall, not to be tried, but baited rather; and then it would have been some comfort to him to see his friends near him. But we do not find any friend he had about the court, save Peter only, and it would have been better if he had been at a distance. Observe how he fell, and how he got up again by repentance. <div eID="gen24003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24004" type="x-p"/> I. His sin, which is here impartially related, to the honour of the penmen of scripture, who dealt faithfully. Observe, <div eID="gen24004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24005" type="x-p"/> 1. The immediate occasion of Peter's sin. He sat without in the palace, among the servants of the High Priest. Note, Bad company is to many an occasion of sin; and those who needlessly thrust themselves into it, go upon the devil's ground, venture into his crowds, and may expect either to be tempted and ensnared, as Peter was, or to be ridiculed and abused, as his Master was; they scarcely can come out of such company, without guilt or grief, or both. He that would keep God's commandments and his own covenant, must say to evil-doers, <hi type="italic">Depart from me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.115">Ps. cxix. 115</reference>. Peter spoke from his own experience, when he warned his new converts to <hi type="italic">save themselves from that untoward generation;</hi> for he had like to have ruined himself by but going once among them. <div eID="gen24005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24006" type="x-p"/> 2. The temptation to it. He was challenged as a retainer to Jesus of Galilee. First one maid, and then another, and then the rest of the servants, charged it upon him; <hi type="italic">Thou also wert with Jesus of Galilee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.26.69">v. 69</reference>. And again, <hi type="italic">This fellow was with Jesus of Nazareth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.26.71">v. 71</reference>. And again (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.73">v. 73</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou also art one of them, for thy speech betrayeth thee</hi> to be a Galilean; whose dialect and pronunciation differed from that of the other Jews. Happy he whose speech betrays him to be a disciple of Christ, by the holiness and seriousness of whose discourse it appears that he has been with Jesus! Observe how scornfully they speak of Christ-Jesus <hi type="italic">of Galilee,</hi> and <hi type="italic">of Nazareth,</hi> upbraiding him with the country he was of: and how disdainfully they speak of Peter—<hi type="italic">This fellow;</hi> as if they thought it a reproach to them to have such a man in their company, and he was well enough served for coming among them; yet they had nothing to accuse him of, but that he was with Jesus, which, they thought, was enough to render him both a scandalous and a suspected person. <div eID="gen24006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24007" type="x-p"/> 3. The sin itself. When he was charged as one of Christ's disciples, he denied it, was ashamed and afraid to own himself so, and would have all about him to believe that he had no knowledge of him, nor any kindness or concern for him. <div eID="gen24007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24008" type="x-p"/> (1.) Upon the first mention of it, he said, <hi type="italic">I know not what thou sayest.</hi> This was a shuffling answer; he pretended that he did not understand the charge, that he knew not whom she meant by <hi type="italic">Jesus of Galilee,</hi> or what she meant by being <hi type="italic">with</hi> him; so making strange of that which his heart was now as full of as it could be. [1.] It is a fault thus to misrepresent our own apprehensions, thoughts, and affections, to serve a turn; to pretend that we do not understand, or did not think of, or remember, that which yet we do apprehend, and did think of, and remember; this is a species of lying which we are more prone to than any other, because in this a man is not easily disproved; for <hi type="italic">who knows the spirit of a man, save himself?</hi> But God knows it, and we must be restrained from this wickedness by a fear of him, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.12">Prov. xxiv. 12</reference>. [2.] It is yet a greater fault to be shy of Christ, to dissemble our knowledge of him, and to shift off a confession of him, when we are called to it; it is, in effect, to <hi type="italic">deny</hi> him. <div eID="gen24008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24009" type="x-p"/> (2.) Upon the next attack, he said, flat and plain, <hi type="italic">I know not the man,</hi> and backed it with an oath, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.72">v. 72</reference>. This was, in effect, to say, I will not own him, I am no Christian; for Christianity is the knowledge of Christ. Why, Peter? Canst thou look upon yonder Prisoner at the bar, and say thou dost not know him? Didst not thou quit all to follow him? And hast thou not been the man of his counsel? Hast thou not known him better than any one else? Didst thou not confess him to be the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? Hast thou forgotten all the kind and tender looks thou hast had from him, and all the intimate fellowship thou hast had with him? Canst thou look him in the face, and say that thou dost not know him? <div eID="gen24009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24010" type="x-p"/> (3.) Upon the third assault, <hi type="italic">he began to curse and to swear, saying, I know not the man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.26.74">v. 74</reference>. This was worst of all, for the way of sin is down-hill. He cursed and swore, [1.] To back what he said, and to gain credit to it, that they might not any more call it in question; he did not only <hi type="italic">say</hi> it, but <hi type="italic">swear</hi> it; and yet what he said, was false. Note, We have reason to suspect the truth of that which is backed with rash oaths and imprecations. None but the devil's sayings need the devil's proofs. He that will not be restrained by the third commandment from mocking his God, will not be kept by the ninth from deceiving his brother. [2.] He designed it to be an evidence for him, that he was none of Christ's disciples, for this was none of their language. Cursing and swearing suffice to prove a man no disciple of Christ; for it is the language of his enemies thus to <hi type="italic">take his name in vain.</hi> <div eID="gen24010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24011" type="x-p"/> This is written for warning to us, that we sin not after the similitude of Peter's transgression; that we never, either directly or indirectly, deny Christ the Lord that bought us, by rejecting his offers, resisting his Spirit, dissembling our knowledge of him, and being ashamed of him and his words, or afraid of suffering for him and with his suffering people. <div eID="gen24011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24012" type="x-p"/> 4. The aggravations of this sin, which it may be of use to take notice of, that we may observe the like transgressions in our own sins. Consider, (1.) Who he was: an apostle, one of the first three, that had been upon all occasions the most forward to speak to the honour of Christ. The greater profession we make of religion, the greater is our sin if in any thing we walk unworthily. (2.) What fair warning his Master had given him of his danger; if he had regarded this as he ought to have done, he would not have run himself into the temptation. (3.) How solemnly he had promised to adhere to Christ in this night of trial; he had said again and again, "<hi type="italic">I will never deny thee;</hi> no, I will die with thee first;" yet he broke these bonds in sunder, and his word was yea and nay. (4.) How soon he fell into this sin after the Lord's supper. There to receive such an inestimable pledge of redeeming love, and yet the same night, before morning, to disown his Redeemer, was indeed <hi type="italic">turning aside quickly.</hi> (5.) How weak comparatively the temptation was; it was not the judge, nor any of the officers of the court, that charged him with being a disciple of Jesus, but a silly maid or two, that probably designed him no hurt, nor would have done him any if he had owned it. This was but <hi type="italic">running with the footmen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">Jer. xii. 5</reference>. (6.) How often he repeated it; even after the cock had crowed once he continued in the temptation, and a second and third time relapsed into the sin. Is this Peter? <hi type="italic">How art thou fallen!</hi> <div eID="gen24012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24013" type="x-p"/> Thus was his sin aggravated; but on the other hand there is this to extenuate it, that, what he said he said <hi type="italic">in his haste,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.116.11">Ps. cxvi. 11</reference>. He fell into the sin by surprise, not as Judas, with design; his heart was against it; he spoke very ill, but it was unadvisedly, and before he was aware. <div eID="gen24013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24014" type="x-p"/> II. Peter's repentance for this sin, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.75">v. 75</reference>. The former is written for our admonition, that we may not sin; but, if at any time we be overtaken, this is written for our imitation, that we may make haste to repent. Now observe, <div eID="gen24014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24015" type="x-p"/> 1. What it was, that brought Peter to repentance. <div eID="gen24015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24016" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">The cock crew</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.74">v. 74</reference>); a common contingency; but, Christ having mentioned the crowing of <hi type="italic">the cock</hi> in the warning he gave him, that made it a means of bringing him to himself. The word of Christ can put a significancy upon whatever sign he shall please to choose, and by virtue of that word he can make it very beneficial to the souls of his people. The crowing of a cock is to Peter instead of a John Baptist, the voice of one calling to repentance. Conscience should be to us as the crowing of the cock, to put us in mind of what we had forgotten. When <hi type="italic">David's heart smote him</hi> the cock crew. Where there is a living principle of grace in the soul, though for the present overpowered by temptation, a little hint will serve, only for a memorandum, when God sets in with it, to recover it from a by-path. Here was the crowing of a cock made a happy occasion of the conversion of a soul. Christ comes sometimes in mercy <hi type="italic">at cock-crowing.</hi> <div eID="gen24016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24017" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">He remembered the words of the Lord;</hi> this was it that brought him to himself, and melted him into tears of godly sorrow; a sense of his ingratitude to Christ, and the slight regard he had had to the gracious warning Christ had given him. Note, A serious reflection upon the words of the Lord Jesus will be a powerful inducement to repentance, and will help to break the heart for sin. Nothing grieves a penitent more than that he has sinned against the grace of the Lord Jesus and the tokens of his love. <div eID="gen24017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24018" type="x-p"/> 2. How his repentance was expressed; <hi type="italic">He went out, and wept bitterly.</hi> <div eID="gen24018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24019" type="x-p"/> (1.) His sorrow was secret; he went out, out of the High Priest's hall, vexed at himself that ever he came into it, now that he found what a snare he was in, and got out of it as fast as he could. He went out into the porch before (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.71">v. 71</reference>); and if he had gone quite off then, his second and third denial had been prevented; but then he came in again, now he went out and came in no more. He went out to some place of solitude and retirement, where he might <hi type="italic">bemoan</hi> himself, <hi type="italic">like the doves of the valleys,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.16">Ezek. vii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.1-Jer.9.2">Jer. ix. 1, 2</reference>. He went out, that he might not be disturbed in his devotions on this sad occasion. We may <hi type="italic">then</hi> be most free in our communion with God, when we are most free from the converse and business of this world. In mourning for sin, we find <hi type="italic">the families apart, and their wives apart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.12.11-Zech.12.12">Zech. xii. 11, 12</reference>. <div eID="gen24019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24020" type="x-p"/> (2.) His sorrow was serious; <hi type="italic">He wept bitterly.</hi> Sorrow for sin must not be slight, but great and deep, like that for an only son. Those that have sinned sweetly, must weep bitterly; for, sooner or later, sin will be bitterness. This deep sorrow is requisite, not to satisfy divine justice (a sea of tears would not do that), but to evidence that there is a real change of mind, which is the essence of repentance, to make the pardon the more welcome, and sin for the future the more loathsome. Peter, who wept so bitterly for denying Christ, never denied him again, but <hi type="italic">confessed</hi> him often and openly, and in the mouth of danger; so far from ever saying, <hi type="italic">I know not the man,</hi> that he made all the house of <hi type="italic">Israel know assuredly that this same Jesus was Lord and Christ.</hi> True repentance for any sin will be best evidenced by our abounding in the contrary grace and duty; that is a sign of our weeping, not only bitterly, but sincerely. Some of the ancients say, that as long as Peter lived, he never heard a cock crow but it set him a weeping. Those that have truly sorrowed for sin, will sorrow upon every remembrance of it; yet not so as to hinder, but rather to increase, their joy in God and in his mercy and grace.  <chapter eID="Matt.26"/> <div eID="gen24020" type="x-p"/>

entries.c091b3c44586b2753def494170442a50ec54e331: <chapter n="26" osisID="Matt.26" sID="Matt.26"/><div eID="gen26516" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13820"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 26</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.26.1-Matt.26.16">Mt 26:1-16</reference>. Christ's Final Announcement of his Death, as Now within Two Days, and the Simultaneous Conspiracy of the Jewish Authorities to Compass It--The Anointing at Bethany--Judas Agrees with the Chief Priests to Betray His Lord. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.14.1-Mark.14.11">Mr 14:1-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.1-Luke.22.6">Lu 22:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.1-John.12.11">Joh 12:1-11</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26517" type="x-p"/> For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.14.1-Mark.14.11">Mr 14:1-11</reference>.<div eID="gen26517" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.26.17-Matt.26.30">Mt 26:17-30</reference>. Preparation for and Last Celebration of the Passover Announcement of the Traitor, and Institution of the Supper. entries.b8bf66ae4c0302ef498d0a2deee6e537d0426694: <div eID="gen38640" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen38641" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen38642" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen38642" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen38641" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen38643" type="x-p"/> Christ predicts his being betrayed and crucified, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.1">Mat 26:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.2">Mat 26:2</reference>. The chief priests, scribes, and elders consult about his death, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.3-Mat.26.5">Mat 26:3-5</reference>. A woman anoints his head at Bethany, at which the disciples are offended, but Christ vindicates her conduct, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.6-Mat.26.13">Mat 26:6-13</reference>. Judas, for thirty pieces of silver, engages with the chief priests to betray him, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.14-Mat.26.16">Mat 26:14-16</reference>. He eats a passover with his disciples, and assures them of his approaching death, and that one of them would betray him, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.17-Mat.26.21">Mat 26:17-21</reference>. On each asking, Is it I? Christ asserts that Judas is the traitor, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.22-Mat.26.25">Mat 26:22-25</reference>. Having eaten his last supper, he institutes the eucharist, to be observed in his Church as a memorial of his sacrificial death, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.26-Mat.26.29">Mat 26:26-29</reference>. They sing a hymn, go to the mount of Olives, and he again announces his approaching death and resurrection, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.30-Mat.26.32">Mat 26:30-32</reference>. Peter asserts his resolution to be faithful to his Master, and Christ foretells his denial and apostasy, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.33-Mat.26.35">Mat 26:33-35</reference>. He goes to Gethsemane; the transactions there, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.36-Mat.26.46">Mat 26:36-46</reference>. Judas comes with the high priest's mob and betrays him with a kiss, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.47-Mat.26.50">Mat 26:47-50</reference>. Peter cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant; Christ discourses with the multitude, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.51-Mat.26.55">Mat 26:51-55</reference>. The disciples flee, and he is led to Caiaphas, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.56">Mat 26:56</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.57">Mat 26:57</reference>. Peter follows at a distance, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.58">Mat 26:58</reference>. They seek false witnesses, and question our Lord, who declares himself to be the Christ, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.59-Mat.26.64">Mat 26:59-64</reference>. They accuse him of blasphemy, and abuse him, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.65-Mat.26.68">Mat 26:65-68</reference>. Peter's denial and repentance, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.69-Mat.26.75">Mat 26:69-75</reference>. <div eID="gen38643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38644" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen38644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38645" type="x-p"/> When Jesus had finished all these sayings - He began these sayings on Mount Olivet, <reference osisRef="Mat.24.1">Mat 24:1</reference>, and continued them till be entered into Bethany, whither he was going.
entries.872d9a38a2f20e12fda992ab313142bc94a8b234: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen38645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38646" type="x-p"/> The passover - A feast instituted in Egypt, to commemorate the destroying angel's passing over the houses of the Israelites, when he slew the firstborn of the Egyptians. See the whole of this business largely explained in the Notes on Exodus 12:1-27 (note). This feast began on the fourteenth day of the first moon, in the first month, Nisan, and it lasted only one day; but it was immediately followed by the days of unleavened bread, which were seven, so that the whole lasted eight days, and all the eight days are sometimes called the feast of the passover, and sometimes the feast or days of unleavened bread. See <reference osisRef="Luk.22.1-Luk.22.7">Luk 22:1-7</reference>. The three most signal benefits vouchsafed to the Israelites were, <div eID="gen38646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38647" type="x-p"/> 1. The deliverance from the slavery of Egypt; to commemorate which they kept the feast of unleavened bread, and the passover. <div eID="gen38647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38648" type="x-p"/> 2. The giving of the law; to commemorate which, they kept the feast of weeks. <div eID="gen38648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38649" type="x-p"/> 3. Their sojourning in the wilderness, and entrance into the promised land; to commemorate which, they kept the feast of tabernacles. <div eID="gen38649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38650" type="x-p"/> See these largely explained, <reference osisRef="Exo.23.14">Exo 23:14</reference> (note); Leviticus 23:2-40 (note). <div eID="gen38650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38651" type="x-p"/> The Son of man is betrayed, (rather delivered up), to be crucified - With what amazing calmness and precision does our blessed Lord speak of this awful event! What a proof does he here give of his prescience in so correctly predicting it; and of his love in so cheerfully undergoing it! Having instructed his disciples and the Jews by his discourses, edified them by his example, convinced them by his miracles, he now prepares to redeem them by his blood! These two verses have no proper connection with this chapter, and should be joined to the preceding.
entries.bbe06df010095b8e19c0e31d8ba5007db04c10dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen38651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38652" type="x-p"/> Then assembled together the chief priests - That is, during the two days that preceded the passover. <div eID="gen38652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38653" type="x-p"/> The high priest, who was called Caiaphas - Caiaphas succeeded Simon, son of Camith, about a.d. 16, or, as Calmet thinks, 25. He married the daughter of Annas, who was joined with him in the priesthood. About two years after our Lord's crucifixion, Caiaphas and Pilate were both deposed by Vitellius, then governor of Syria, and afterwards emperor. Caiaphas, unable to bear this disgrace, and the stings of his conscience for the murder of Christ, killed himself about a.d. 35. See Joseph. Ant. b. xviii. c. 2-4.
entries.0ed9b67d2c08e5220c65a8afbe69726680134455: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen38653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38654" type="x-p"/> And consulted that they might take Jesus by subtilty - The providence of God frustrated their artful machinations; and that event which they wished to conduct with the greatest privacy and silence was transacted with all possible celebrity, amidst the thousands who resorted to Jerusalem, at this season, for the keeping of the passover. It was, doubtless, of the very first importance that the crucifixion of Christ, which was preparatory to the most essential achievement of Christianity, viz. his resurrection from the grave, should be exhibited before many witnesses, and in the most open manner, that infidelity might not attempt, in future, to invalidate the evidences of the Christian religion, by alleging that these things were done in a corner. See Wakefield in loco.
entries.64ca5b3704b2ea6246640f2c17758848a8785e10: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen38654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38655" type="x-p"/> Not on the feast day, lest there be an uproar - It was usual for the Jews to punish criminals at the public festivals; but in this case they were afraid of an insurrection, as our Lord had become very popular. The providence of God directed it thus, for the reason given in the preceding note. <div eID="gen38655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38656" type="x-p"/> He who observes a festival on motives purely human violates it in his heart, and is a hypocrite before God. It is likely they feared the Galileans, as being the countrymen of our Lord, more than they feared the people of Jerusalem.
entries.c8196e0ed20c71bab8c2a7a350aa0bdaf500c029: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen38656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38657" type="x-p"/> In Bethany - For a solution of the difficulties in this verse, about the time of the anointing, see the observations at the end of this chapter. <div eID="gen38657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38658" type="x-p"/> Simon the Leper - This was probably no more than a surname, as Simon the Canaanite, <reference osisRef="Mat.10.4">Mat 10:4</reference>, and Barsabas Justus, <reference osisRef="Act.1.23">Act 1:23</reference>, and several others. Yet it might have been some person that Christ had healed of this disease. See <reference osisRef="Mat.11.5">Mat 11:5</reference>.
entries.f2d87e304c098a89fb24f5f92205014457e593ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen38658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38659" type="x-p"/> There came unto him a woman - There is much contention among commentators about the transaction mentioned here, and in <reference osisRef="Joh.12.3">Joh 12:3</reference>; some supposing them to be different, others to be the same. Bishop Newcome's view of the subject I have placed at the end of the chapter. <div eID="gen38659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38660" type="x-p"/> Some think that the woman mentioned here was Mary, the sister of Lazarus; others Mary Magdalene; but against the former opinion it is argued that it is not likely, had this been Mary the sister of Lazarus, that Matthew and Mark would have suppressed her name. Besides, say they, we should not confound the repast which is mentioned here, with that mentioned by John, <reference osisRef="Joh.12.3">Joh 12:3</reference>. This one was made only two days before the passover, and that one six days before: the one was made at the house of Simon the leper, the other at the house of Lazarus, <reference osisRef="Joh.12.1">Joh 12:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.12.2">Joh 12:2</reference>. At this, the woman poured the oil on the head of Christ; at the other, Mary anointed Christ's feet with it. See on <reference osisRef="Mar.14.3">Mar 14:3</reference> (note), and see the notes at the end of this chapter, (Bishop Newcome's Account of the Anointing).
entries.498bb8bb8df8abcbcc1e807124dd4b7383031c25: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen38660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38661" type="x-p"/> His disciples - One of them, viz. Judas. This mode of speaking was common among the Hebrews. So, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.44">Mat 27:44</reference>, the thieves also, i.e. one of them. So, <reference osisRef="Mat.28.17">Mat 28:17</reference>, some doubted, i.e. one, Thomas. See also <reference osisRef="Gen.8.4">Gen 8:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jdg.12.7">Jdg 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.6.7">Neh 6:7</reference>, etc. By a figure called among rhetoricians enallag, the plural is put for the singular; it is, however, possible that Judas, who made the objection, was followed in the sentiment by the rest of the disciples.
entries.28726b7d8e4e4acd9348cf464dcbad43a8d9db46: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen38661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38662" type="x-p"/> And given to the poor - How often does charity serve as a cloak for covetousness! God is sometimes robbed of his right under the pretense of devoting what is withheld to some charitable purpose, to which there was no intention ever to give it.
entries.65f8dfc79cde56cf3dc4222715287cc6772f6279: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen38662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38663" type="x-p"/> Why trouble ye the woman? - Or, Why do ye put the woman to pain? See this sense of κοπους παρεχειν, established by Kypke in loco. A generous mind is ever pained when it is denied the opportunity of doing good, or when its proffered kindness is refused.
entries.29c5f4c105d9914bd1b2af68577ff01601bbacd1: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen38663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38664" type="x-p"/> Ye have the poor always with you - And, consequently, have the opportunity of doing them good at any time; but me ye have not always; my bodily presence is about to be removed from you for ever. The woman, under a presentiment of my death is preparing me for my burial.
entries.b4e2b935567b98fcf368ae9a163c6fe6116e51f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen38664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38665" type="x-p"/> She did it for my burial - Or, She hath done it to embalm me - ενταφιασαι με. The Septuagint use ενταφιαϚης for the person whose office it was to embalm, <reference osisRef="Gen.50.2">Gen 50:2</reference>, and ενταφιαζω for the Hebrew הנט which signifies to prepare with spices, or aromatics, <reference osisRef="Gen.50.3">Gen 50:3</reference>. Our Lord took this opportunity to tell them, once more, that he was shortly to die.
entries.17d8380645a89a4197a5e694133e31fbcf04f304: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen38665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38666" type="x-p"/> Wheresoever this Gospel shall be preached - Another remarkable proof of the prescience of Christ. Such a matter as this, humanly speaking, depended on mere fortuitous circumstances, yet so has God disposed matters, that the thing has continued, hitherto, as firm and regular as the ordinances of heaven. <div eID="gen38666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38667" type="x-p"/> For a memorial of her - As embalming preserves the body from corruption, and she has done this good work to embalm and preserve this body, so will I order every thing concerning this transaction to be carefully recorded, to preserve her memory to the latest ages. The actions which the world blames, through the spirit of envy, covetousness, or malice, God takes delight to distinguish and record.
entries.5c4ccc297c3b75e30ac0b0e1c9f4636e4d599d3c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen38667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38668" type="x-p"/> Then - Judas - After this supper at Bethany, Judas returned to Jerusalem, and made his contract with the chief priests.
entries.bc8bd75537d7f753ffe7ec08152213e56b3885e4: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen38668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38669" type="x-p"/> Thirty pieces of silver - Τριακοντα αργυρια, thirty silverlings; but στατηρας, staters, is the reading of the Codex Bezae, three copies of the Itala, Eusebius, and Origen sometimes; and στατηρας αργυριου, silver staters, is the reading of the famous Basil MS. No. 1, in Griesbach, and one copy of the Itala. <div eID="gen38669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38670" type="x-p"/> A stater was the same as the shekel, and worth about 3s. English money, according to Dean Prideaux: a goodly price for the Savior of the world! Thirty staters, about 4l. 10s. the common price for the meanest slave! See <reference osisRef="Exo.21.32">Exo 21:32</reference>. The rabbins say, thirty סלעין selain of pure silver was the standard price for a slave, whether good or bad, male or female. See tract Erachin, fol. 14, and Shekalim, cap. 1. Each selaa weighed 384 barley-corns; the same number was contained in a shekel; and therefore the shekel and the selaa were the same. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.20.16">Gen 20:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Exo.38.24">Exo 38:24</reference>.
entries.3c3ba25df57e63c1d2b9e28d44036f8c7f26935a: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen38670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38671" type="x-p"/> He sought opportunity - Ευκαιριαν, a convenient or fit opportunity. Men seldom leave a crime imperfect: when once sin is conceived, it meets, in general, with few obstacles, till it brings forth death. How deceitful, how deeply damning, is the love of money! Well might a heathen exclaim, while contemplating the grave of a person who was murdered for the sake of his wealth: - - Quid non mortalia pectora cogis Auri Sacra Fames? <div eID="gen38671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38672" type="x-p"/> Virg. Aen. iii. 56 "O! cursed lust of gold! what wilt thou not compel the human heart to perpetrate?" <div eID="gen38672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38673" type="x-p"/> Judas is deservedly considered as one of the most infamous of men, his conduct base beyond description, and his motives vile. But how many, since his time, have walked in the same way! How many, for the sake of worldly wealth, have renounced the religion of their Lord and Master, and sold Jesus, and their interest in heaven, for a short-lived portion of secular good! From <reference osisRef="Joh.12.6">Joh 12:6</reference>, we learn that Judas, who was treasurer to our Lord and his disciples, (for he carried the bag), was a thief, and frequently purloined a portion of what was given for the support of this holy family. Being disappointed of the prey he hoped to have from the sale of the precious ointment, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.9">Mat 26:9</reference>, he sold his Master to make up the sum. A thorough Jew!
entries.648f9f17754146b41e0f0aba82f521e0e564bc0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen38673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38674" type="x-p"/> Now the first day of the feast of unleavened bread - As the feast of unleavened bread did not begin till the day after the passover, the fifteenth day of the month, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.5">Lev 23:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.6">Lev 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.28.16">Num 28:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.28.17">Num 28:17</reference>, this could not have been, properly, the first day of that feast; but as the Jews began to eat unleavened bread on the fourteenth, <reference osisRef="Exo.12.18">Exo 12:18</reference>, this day was often termed the first of unleavened bread. The evangelists use it in this sense, and call even the paschal day by this name. See <reference osisRef="Mar.14.12">Mar 14:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.22.7">Luk 22:7</reference>. <div eID="gen38674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38675" type="x-p"/> Where wilt thou that we prepare - How astonishing is this, that He who created all things, whether visible or invisible, and by whom all things were upheld, should so empty himself as not to be proprietor of a single house in his whole creation, to eat the last passover with his disciples! This is certainly a mystery, and so, less or more is every thing that God does. But how inveterate and destructive must the nature of sin be, when such emptying and humiliation were necessary to its destruction! It is worthy of note what the Talmudists say, that the inhabitants of Jerusalem did not let out their houses to those who came to the annual feasts; but afforded all accommodations of this kind gratis. A man might therefore go and request the use of any room, on such an occasion, which was as yet unoccupied. The earthen jug, and the skin of the sacrifice, were left with the host. See Lightfoot, vol. ii. p. 21.
entries.91047f5a4f0d648f2ebe3a46fa94a38c5fa7ab85: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen38675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38676" type="x-p"/> Go - to such a man - Τον δεινα It is probable that this means some person with whom Christ was well acquainted, and who was known to the disciples. Grotius observes that the Greeks use this form when they mean some particular person who is so well known that there is no need to specify him by name. The circumstances are more particularly marked in <reference osisRef="Luk.22.8">Luk 22:8</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen38676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38677" type="x-p"/> My time is at hand - That is, the time of my crucifixion. Kypke has largely shown that καιρος is often used among the Greeks for affliction and calamity. It might be rendered here, the time of my crucifixion is at hand.
entries.96cf398231cf8f73e3e9d304183ae9f1cfde3745: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen38677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38678" type="x-p"/> And the disciples did - The disciples that were sent on this errand were Peter and John. See <reference osisRef="Luk.22.8">Luk 22:8</reference>. <div eID="gen38678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38679" type="x-p"/> They made ready the passover - That is, they provided the lamb, etc., which were appointed by the law for this solemnity. Mr. Wakefield justly observes, "that the Jews considered the passover as a sacrificial rite; Josephus calls it θυσιαν, A Sacrifice; and Trypho, in Justin Martyr, speaks of προβατον του πασχα θυειν, Sacrificing the paschal lamb. But what comes nearer to the point is this, that Maimonides, one of the most eminent of the Jewish rabbins, has a particular treatise on the paschal sacrifice; and throughout that piece, speaks of the lamb as a victim, and of the solemnity itself as a sacrifice. And R. Bechai, in his commentary on <reference osisRef="Lev.2.11">Lev 2:11</reference>, says that the paschal sacrifice was of a piacular nature, in order to expiate the guilt contracted by the idolatrous practices of the Israelites in Egypt." It was highly necessary that this should be considered as an expiatory sacrifice, as it typified that Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. For much more on this important subject than can, with propriety, be introduced into these notes, see a Discourse on the Eucharist, lately published by the author of this work.
entries.fff5581828b178660eef61f83860666430021a7e: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen38679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38680" type="x-p"/> Now when the even was come, he sat down with the twelve. - It is a common opinion that our Lord ate the passover some hours before the Jews ate it; for the Jews, according to custom, ate theirs at the end of the fourteenth day, but Christ ate his the preceding even, which was the beginning of the same sixth day, or Friday; the Jews begin their day at sunsetting, we at midnight. Thus Christ ate the passover on the same day with the Jews, but not on the same hour. Christ kept this passover the beginning of the fourteenth day, the precise day and hour in which the Jews had eaten their first passover in Egypt. See <reference osisRef="Exo.12.6-Exo.12.12">Exo 12:6-12</reference>. And in the same part of the same day in which the Jews had sacrificed their first paschal lamb, viz. between the two evenings, about the ninth hour, or 3 o'clock, Jesus Christ our passover was sacrificed for us: for it was at this hour that he yielded up his last breath; and then it was that, the sacrifice being completed, Jesus said, It Is Finished. See <reference osisRef="Exo.12.6">Exo 12:6</reference>, etc., and <reference osisRef="Deu.16.6">Deu 16:6</reference>, etc. See on <reference osisRef="Joh.18.28">Joh 18:28</reference> (note), and the Treatise on the Eucharist, referred to <reference osisRef="Mat.26.19">Mat 26:19</reference>; and see the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.26.26">Mat 26:26</reference> and following verses.
entries.8b45d2c28cb2959f0bce3521ad7d6d405c01ede9: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen38680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38681" type="x-p"/> One of you shall betray me - Or, will deliver me up. Judas had already betrayed him, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.15">Mat 26:15</reference>, and he was now about to deliver him into the hands of the chief priests, according to the agreement he had made with them.
entries.37183d6be23478250d4a5c2276fb2d380807bceb: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen38681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38682" type="x-p"/> They were exceeding sorrowful - That is, the eleven who were innocent; and the hypocritical traitor, Judas, endeavored to put on the appearance of sorrow. Strange! Did he not know that Christ knew the secrets of his soul! Or had his love of money so far blinded him, as to render him incapable of discerning even this, with which he had been before so well acquainted?
entries.d00757edfd25bce425770be09bbb653a2747486e: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen38682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38683" type="x-p"/> He that dippeth his hand - As the Jews ate the passover a whole family together, it was not convenient for them all to dip their bread in the same dish; they therefore had several little dishes or plates, in which was the juice of the bitter herbs, mentioned <reference osisRef="Exo.12.8">Exo 12:8</reference>, on different parts of the table; and those who were nigh one of these, dipped their bread in it. As Judas is represented as dipping in the same dish with Christ, it shows that he was either near or opposite to him. If this man's heart had not been hardened, and his conscience seared beyond all precedent, by the deceitfulness of his sin, would he have showed his face in this sacred assembly, or have thus put the seal to his own perdition, by eating of this sacrificial lamb? Is it possible that he could feel no compunction? Alas! having delivered himself up into the hands of the devil, he was capable of delivering up his Master into the hands of the chief priests; and thus, when men are completely hardened by the deceitfulness of sin, they can outwardly perform the most solemn acts of devotion, without feeling any sort of inward concern about the matter.
entries.7ad96b2927bed6a2e007d75766cb1ba8ea31be5b: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen38683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38684" type="x-p"/> The Son of man goeth - That is, is about to die. Going, going away, departing, etc., are frequently used in the best Greek and Latin writers, for death, or dying. The same words are often used in the Scriptures in the same sense. <div eID="gen38684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38685" type="x-p"/> It had been good for that man - Can this be said of any sinner, in the common sense in which it is understood, if there be any redemption from hell's torments? If a sinner should suffer millions of millions of years in them, and get out at last to the enjoyment of heaven, then it was well for him that he had been born, for still he has an eternity of blessedness before him. Can the doctrine of the non-eternity of hell's torments stand in the presence of this saying? Or can the doctrine of the annihilation of the wicked consist with this declaration? It would have been well for that man if he had never been born! Then he must be in some state of conscious existence, as non-existence is said to be better than that state in which he is now found. It was common for the Jews to say of any flagrant transgressor, It would have been better for him had he never been born. See several examples in Schoettgen. See the case of Judas argued at the end of Acts 1 (note).
entries.b8a5c3fdce2930e76227bf199f006963f9e9fcf2: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen38685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38686" type="x-p"/> Judas - said, Master, is it I? - What excessive impudence! He knew, in his conscience, that he had already betrayed his Master, and was waiting now for the servants of the chief priests, that he might deliver him into their hands; and yet he says, (hoping that he had transacted his business so privately that it had not yet transpired), Master, is it I? It is worthy of remark, that each of the other disciples said κυριε, Lord, is it I? But Judas dares not, or will not, use this august title, but simply says ραββι, Teacher, is it I? <div eID="gen38686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38687" type="x-p"/> Thou hast said - Συ ειπας, or אתון אמריתון atun amaritun, "Ye have said," was a common form of expression for Yes. It Is so. "When the Zipporenses inquired whether Rabbi Judas was dead? the son of Kaphra answered, Ye have said," i.e. He is dead. See Schoettgen. Hor. Hebr. p.
entries.5caaee0269dfe2ea5c17dadf773a84f1a528043e: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen38687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38688" type="x-p"/> Jesus took bread - This is the first institution of what is termed the Lord's Supper. To every part of this ceremony, as here mentioned, the utmost attention should be paid. <div eID="gen38688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38689" type="x-p"/> To do this, in the most effectual manner, I think it necessary to set down the text of the three evangelists who have transmitted the whole account, collated with that part of St. Paul's First Epistle to the Corinthians which speaks of the same subject, and which, he assures us, he received by Divine revelation. It may seem strange that, although John (13:1-38) mentions all the circumstances preceding the holy supper, and, from 14:1-31 the circumstances which succeeded the breaking of the bread, and in chapters 15, 16, and 17, the discourse which followed the administration of the cup; yet he takes no notice of the Divine institution at all. This is generally accounted for on his knowledge of what the other three evangelists had written; and on his conviction that their relation was true, and needed no additional confirmation, as the matter was amply established by the conjoint testimony of three such respectable witnesses. <reference osisRef="Mat.26.26">Mat 26:26</reference> <reference osisRef="Mar.14.22">Mar 14:22</reference> <reference osisRef="Luk.22.19">Luk 22:19</reference> <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.23-1Cor.11.24">1Cor 11:23-24</reference> And as they were eating, Jesus took bread and blessed it (ευλογησας and blessed God) and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat, this is my body. And as they did eat, Jesus took bread and blessed (ευλογησας, blessed God) and brake it, and to them, and said, Take, eat, this is my body. And he took bread and gave thanks, (ευχαριϚησας, i.e. to God), and gave brake it, and gave unto them, saying: This is my body which is given for you: This do in remembrance of me. The Lord Jesus, the same night in which he was betrayed, took bread; And when he had given thanks (και ευχαριϚησος, i.e. to God) he brake it, and said, Take, eat, this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me. <div eID="gen38689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38690" type="x-p"/> After giving the bread, the discourse related, John 14:1-31, inclusive, is supposed by Bishop Newcome to have been delivered by our Lord, for the comfort and support of his disciples under their present and approaching trials. <reference osisRef="Mat.26.27-Mat.26.29">Mat 26:27-29</reference> <reference osisRef="Mar.14.23-Mar.14.25">Mar 14:23-25</reference> <reference osisRef="Luk.22.20">Luk 22:20</reference> <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.25">1Cor 11:25</reference> And he took the cup, and gave thanks (ευχαριϚησας), and gave it to them, saying: Drink ye all of it. And he took the cup; and when he had given thanks, (ευχαριϚησας), he gave it to them; and they all drank of it. Likewise also the cup, after supper, saying: After the same manner also, he took the cup, when he had supped, saying: For this is my blood of the New Testament, which is shed for many or the remission of sins. And he said unto them, This is my blood of the New Testament, which is shed for many. This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which is shed for you. This cup is the New Testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me. But I say unto you, I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom. Verily I say unto you, I will drink no more of the fruit of the vine until that day that I drink it new in the kingdom of God. <div eID="gen38690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38691" type="x-p"/> After this, our Lord resumes that discourse which is found in the 15th, 16th, and 17th chapters of John, beginning with the last verse of chap. 14, Arise, let us go hence. Then succeed the following words, which conclude the whole ceremony. <reference osisRef="Mat.26.30">Mat 26:30</reference> <reference osisRef="Mar.14.26">Mar 14:26</reference> <reference osisRef="Luk.22.39">Luk 22:39</reference> <reference osisRef="Joh.14.1">Joh 14:1</reference> And when they had sung a hymn, they went out into the Mount of Olives. And when they had sung a hymn, they went out into the Mount of Olives. And he came out, and went as he was wont to the Mount of Olives. And his disciples also followed him. When Jesus had spoken these words, he went forth with his disciples over the brook Kedron. <div eID="gen38691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38692" type="x-p"/> From the preceding harmonized view of this important transaction, as described by three Evangelists and one Apostle, we see the first institution, nature, and design of what has been since called The Lord's Supper. To every circumstance, as set down here, and the mode of expression by which such circumstances are described, we should pay the deepest attention. <div eID="gen38692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38693" type="x-p"/> As they were eating - Either an ordinary supper, or the paschal lamb, as some think. See the observations at the end of this chapter. <div eID="gen38693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38694" type="x-p"/> Jesus took bread - Of what kind? Unleavened bread, certainly, because there was no other kind to be had in all Judea at this time; for this was the first day of unleavened bread, (<reference osisRef="Mat.26.17">Mat 26:17</reference>), i.e. the 14th of the month Nisan, when the Jews, according to the command of God, (<reference osisRef="Exo.12.15-Exo.12.20">Exo 12:15-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.23.15">Exo 23:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.34.25">Exo 34:25</reference>), were to purge away all leaven from their houses; for he who sacrificed the passover, having leaven in his dwelling, was considered to be such a transgressor of the Divine law as could no longer be tolerated among the people of God; and therefore was to be cut off from the congregation of Israel. Leo of Modena, who has written a very sensible treatise on the customs of the Jews, observes, "That so strictly do some of the Jews observe the precept concerning the removal of all leaven from their houses, during the celebration of the paschal solemnity, that they either provide vessels entirely new for baking, or else have a set for the purpose, which are dedicated solely to the service of the passover, and never brought out on any other occasion." <div eID="gen38694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38695" type="x-p"/> To this divinely instituted custom of removing all leaven previously to the paschal solemnity, St. Paul evidently alludes, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.6-1Cor.5.8">1Cor 5:6-8</reference>. Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump? Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ, our passover, is sacrificed for us; therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the Unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. <div eID="gen38695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38696" type="x-p"/> Now, if any respect should be paid to the primitive institution, in the celebration of this Divine ordinance, then, unleavened, unyeasted bread should be used. In every sign, or type, the thing signifying or pointing out that which is beyond itself should either have certain properties, or be accompanied with certain circumstances, as expressive as possible of the thing signified. Bread, simply considered in itself, may be an emblem apt enough of the body of our Lord Jesus, which was given for us; but the design of God was evidently that it should not only point out this, but also the disposition required in those who should celebrate both the antetype and the type; and this the apostle explains to be sincerity and truth, the reverse of malice and wickedness. The very taste of the bread was instructive: it pointed out to every communicant, that he who came to the table of God with malice or ill-will against any soul of man, or with wickedness, a profligate or sinful life, might expect to eat and drink judgment to himself, as not discerning that the Lord's body was sacrificed for this very purpose, that all sin might be destroyed; and that sincerity, ειλικρινεια, such purity as the clearest light can discern no stain in, might be diffused through the whole soul; and that truth, the law of righteousness and true holiness, might regulate and guide all the actions of life. Had the bread used on these occasions been of the common kind, it would have been perfectly unfit, or improper, to have communicated these uncommon significations; and, as it was seldom used, its rare occurrence would make the emblematical representation more deeply impressive; and the sign, and the thing signified, have their due correspondence and influence. <div eID="gen38696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38697" type="x-p"/> These circumstances considered, will it not appear that the use of common bread in the sacrament of the Lord's Supper is highly improper? He who can say, "This is a matter of no importance," may say with equal propriety, the bread itself is of no importance; and another may say, the wine is of no importance; and a third may say, "neither the bread nor wine is any thing, but as they lead to spiritual references; and, the spiritual reference being once understood, the signs are useless." Thus we may, through affected spirituality, refine away the whole ordinance of God; and, with the letter and form of religion, abolish religion itself. Many have already acted in this way, not only to their loss, but to their ruin, by showing how profoundly wise they are above what is written. Let those, therefore, who consider that man shall live by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God, and who are conscientiously solicitous that each Divine institution be not only preserved, but observed in all its original integrity, attend to this circumstance. The Lutheran Church makes use of unleavened bread to the present day. <div eID="gen38697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38698" type="x-p"/> And blessed it - Both St. Matthew and St. Mark use the word ευλογησας, blessed, instead of ευχαριϚησας, gave thanks, which is the word used by St. Luke and St. Paul. But instead of ευλογησας, blessed, ευχαριϚησας, gave thanks, is the reading of ten MSS. in uncial characters, of the Dublin Codex rescriptus, published by Dr. Barrett, and of more than one hundred others, of the greatest respectability. This is the reading also of the Syriac and Arabic, and is confirmed by several of the primitive fathers. The terms, in this case, are nearly of the same import, as both blessing and giving thanks were used on these occasions. But what was it that our Lord blessed? Not the bread, though many think the contrary, being deceived by the word It, which is improperly supplied in our version. In all the four places referred to above, whether the word blessed or gave thanks is used, it refers not to the bread, but to God, the dispenser of every good. Our Lord here conforms himself to that constant Jewish custom, viz. of acknowledging God as the author of every good and perfect gift, by giving thanks on taking the bread and taking the cup at their ordinary meals. For every Jew was forbidden to eat, drink, or use any of God's creatures without rendering him thanks; and he who acted contrary to this command was considered as a person who was guilty of sacrilege. <div eID="gen38698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38699" type="x-p"/> From this custom we have derived the decent and laudable one of saying grace (gratas thanks) before and after meat. The Jewish form of blessing, probably that which our Lord used on this occasion, none of my readers will be displeased to find here, though it has been mentioned once before. On taking the bread they say: - ברוך אתה אלהינו מלך העולם המוצא לחם מן הארץ <div eID="gen38699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38700" type="x-p"/> Baruch atta Elohinoo, Melech, haolam, ha motse Lechem min haarets. <div eID="gen38700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38701" type="x-p"/> Blessed be thou, our God, King of the universe, who bringest forth bread out of the earth! <div eID="gen38701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38702" type="x-p"/> Likewise, on taking the cup, they say: - ברוך אלהינו מלך העולם בורא פרי הגף <div eID="gen38702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38703" type="x-p"/> Baruch Elohinoo, Melech, haolam, Bore perey haggephen. <div eID="gen38703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38704" type="x-p"/> Blessed be our God, the King of the universe, the Creator of the fruit it of the vine! <div eID="gen38704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38705" type="x-p"/> The Mohammedans copy their example, constantly saying before and after meat: - <div eID="gen38705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38706" type="x-p"/> Bismillahi arahmani arraheemi. <div eID="gen38706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38707" type="x-p"/> In the name of God, the most merciful, the most compassionate. <div eID="gen38707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38708" type="x-p"/> No blessing, therefore, of the elements is here intended; they were already blessed, in being sent as a gift of mercy from the bountiful Lord; but God the sender is blessed, because of the liberal provision he has made for his worthless creatures. Blessing and touching the bread are merely Popish ceremonies, unauthorized either by Scripture or the practice of the pure Church of God; necessary of course to those who pretend to transmute, by a kind of spiritual incantation, the bread and wine into the real body and blood of Jesus Christ; a measure the grossest in folly, and most stupid in nonsense, to which God in judgment ever abandoned the fallen spirit of man. <div eID="gen38708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38709" type="x-p"/> And brake it - We often read in the Scriptures of breaking bread, but never of cutting it. The Jewish people had nothing similar to our high-raised loaf: their bread was made broad and thin, and was consequently very brittle, and, to divide it, there was no need of a knife. <div eID="gen38709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38710" type="x-p"/> The breaking of the bread I consider essential to the proper performance of this solemn and significant ceremony: because this act was designed by our Lord to shadow forth the wounding, piercing, and breaking of his body upon the cross; and, as all this was essentially necessary to the making a full atonement for the sin of the world, so it is of vast importance that this apparently little circumstance, the breaking of the bread, should be carefully attended to, that the godly communicant may have every necessary assistance to enable him to discern the Lord's body, while engaged in this most important and Divine of all God's ordinances. But who does not see that one small cube of fermented, i.e. leavened bread, previously divided from the mass with a knife, and separated by the fingers of the minister, can never answer the end of the institution, either as to the matter of the bread, or the mode of dividing it? Man is naturally a dull and heedless creature, especially in spiritual things, and has need of the utmost assistance of his senses, in union with those expressive rites and ceremonies which the Holy Scripture, not tradition, has sanctioned, in order to enable him to arrive at spiritual things, through the medium of earthly similitudes. <div eID="gen38710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38711" type="x-p"/> And gave it to the disciples - Not only the breaking, but also the Distribution, of the bread are necessary parts of this rite. In the Romish Church, the bread is not broken nor delivered to the people, that They may take and eat; but the consecrated wafer is put upon their tongue by the priest; and it is generally understood by the communicants, that they should not masticate, but swallow it whole. "That the breaking of this bread to be distributed," says Dr. Whitby, "is a necessary part of this rite is evident, first, by the continual mention of it by St. Paul and all the evangelists, when they speak of the institution of this sacrament, which shows it to be a necessary part of it. 2dly, Christ says, Take, eat, this is my body, Broken for you, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.24">1Cor 11:24</reference>. But when the elements are not broken, it can be no more said, This is my body broken for you, than where the elements are not given. 3dly, Our Lord said, Do this in remembrance of me: i.e. 'Eat this bread, broken in remembrance of my body broken on the cross:' now, where no body broken is distributed, there, nothing can be eaten in memorial of his broken body. Lastly, The apostle, by saying, The bread which we Break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? sufficiently informs us that the eating of his broken body is necessary to that end, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.10">1Cor 10:10</reference>. Hence it was that this rite, of distributing bread broken, continued for a thousand years, and was, as Humbertus testifies, observed in the Roman Church in the eleventh century." Whitby in loco.
